note: Literature workflow for the looping test (2026-10-19): two search lenses, 18 candidates, 8 read end to end by one agent each, then a synthesis. Machine-written notes; claims are checked in docs/REPRODUCTION.md where used.

candidates.title: Scaling Latent Reasoning via Looped Language Models (Ouro)
candidates.why: This is the closest published test to ours, and it finds that looping does NOT increase knowledge storage. Section 6.1 uses Capo-style synthetic biographies (a name plus 5 attributes) on GPT-2 models of 1M-40M parameters, with 20K-500K individuals and 1000 exposures. Non-looped models (1 step) are compared with 4-step looped models at equal parameters. Both reach about 2 bits/parameter: 'looping does not increase knowledge capacity nor improve capacity scaling.' The gains show up only in knowledge manipulation (Mano tasks and multi-hop QA). Two further points: models trained with at most 4 steps degrade moderately when run at T=5-8, and 8-step training caused loss spikes. Bearing: this is the expected null for L1, and GeGLU's 0.938/0.933/0.926 fits it. Any Cos-Bochner gain would therefore have to be kernel-specific rather than extra capacity. For L4, a wider seen/held-out gap would have to come from reallocating storage to wording, since looping adds no storage. It also warns that K_test=8 > K_train will degrade.

candidates.title: Reasoning with Latent Thoughts: On the Power of Looped Transformers
candidates.why: ICLR 2025. Compares a k-layer block looped L times with iso-parameter and iso-FLOP baselines. Closed-book QA, which the authors treat as memorization, tracks perplexity: its %-gap equals the perplexity %-gap, and the looped model trails the iso-FLOP baseline because memorization depends on parameter count. Open-book QA, math word problems and reasoning primitives benefit disproportionately, which the authors call an inductive bias toward reasoning. A looping-style regularizer (cosine similarity between blocks) leaves closed-book QA roughly unchanged. Bearing: this is the main 'looping does not help recall' prior against L1. Its reasoning-bias story points the other way from L4: if looping changes anything, it should favour wording-invariant use of facts (L5), not wording memorization.

candidates.title: Stability and Generalization in Looped Transformers
candidates.why: Obscure single-author preprint (Labovich). It gives a fixed-point framework that maps directly onto our measures. Our looped block is 'autonomous' in its terms: h <- h + f(LN(h)) with no re-injection of the input and only pre-norm. Prop. 2: for almost all parameterizations, an autonomous loop has a dimension-zero set of isolated fixed points, so its input-dependence reduces to choosing a basin, which is exactly the associative clean-up that L2 assumes. It classifies networks by the Jacobian spectral radius at the fixed point. Below 1, the fixed point is reachable but the input is forgotten. Above 1, fixed points are 'practically never reached'. Near 1 from below, parameter gradients become unstable. Bearing: GeGLU's per-pass radius of about 3.3 is in the expansive regime, so extra passes should drift rather than clean up. L2 and L3 need the radius below 1 near stored states, so the radius should be measured at stored states versus noised states, not only on average.

candidates.title: Hopfield Networks is All You Need (Ramsauer et al.)
candidates.why: The inverse temperature beta, which plays the role of our 1/T bandwidth, decides which fixed point the update reaches: a global average, metastable averages over a subset, or a single stored pattern. For well-separated patterns, retrieval takes one step with error exponentially small in the separation, and the Jacobian bound near a pattern is also exponentially small, so the update is strongly contracting there. For L1 this predicts that narrow Cos-Bochner should already retrieve at K = 1 and gain little from extra passes. Looping should help mainly a wider kernel stuck in metastable mixtures. For L3 it predicts the opposite of the prediction as worded: at stored states a narrow kernel should give the smallest per-pass spectral radius (saturated weights), with large values only near basin boundaries. The paper assumes an auto-associative update that returns a stored pattern. Our block is h + f(LN(h)) with hetero-associative values, so the correspondence holds only if f(LN(h*)) is near zero at the trained states.

candidates.title: Dense Associative Memory Through the Lens of Random Features (DrDAM; Hoover, Chau, Strobelt, Ram, Krotov)
candidates.why: The closest match to the Cos-Bochner FFN. It replaces per-pattern Dense Associative Memory weights with Rahimi-Recht trigonometric (SinCos) random features for the RBF kernel at a fixed parameter count, and checks how well the energy and the retrieval dynamics are approximated. The approximation of the dynamics gets worse as beta grows (error at beta = 50 about 10-100x that at lower beta), as dimension grows, and as the query moves away from stored patterns. At high beta and dimension, adding features does not help. So narrow T = 1 with 4k features in width 128 may not reach the ideal kernel-smoother attractor, and the error should compound under iteration. This is a concrete reason to expect K_test = 8 to degrade, against L1. The noise 0.5 condition, with queries far from stored states, is the worst-approximated regime, against L2.

candidates.title: Kernel Memory Networks: A Unifying Framework for Memory Modeling (Iatropoulos, Brea, Gerstner)
candidates.why: Less widely known NeurIPS paper. It treats recall as kernel classification or interpolation. A hetero-associative feed-forward memory becomes an attractor network only when outputs equal inputs (Xout = Xin), and s <- X K^+ K(X, s) guarantees stored patterns are fixed points. With an exponential-power kernel of scale r, r sets the radius of attraction: noise with norm below r converges in one step, while states farther than r from every pattern collapse to an 'agnostic' state. r trades noise tolerance against capacity. For L2 this predicts a sharp threshold for narrow Cos-Bochner across relative noise 0.1 / 0.25 / 0.5 (clean-up works below the kernel radius and fails above it), and a smoother curve for T = 2. It also warns that our facts FFN is trained hetero-associatively (name state to attribute), so no clean-up toward stored states is guaranteed. Measure |f(LN(h*))| at clean states to check.

candidates.title: A review of mean-shift algorithms for clustering (Carreira-Perpinan)
candidates.why: Technical review covering iterated kernel-weighted averages (mean-shift, Gaussian blurring mean-shift). At a mode, the Jacobian of the update x <- m(x) is J = Sigma(x*)/sigma^2, with eigenvalues in (0, 1). Convergence is nearly superlinear as sigma -> 0 or sigma -> infinity, slow and linear at intermediate bandwidth, and sublinear where modes merge. Early steps are large and later ones small, and blurring mean-shift eventually collapses everything to one point. Mapped to our residual form h <- h + f(h), mode-seeking means J_f close to -I and spectral radius of I + J_f below 1. Our |J - I| and per-pass relative-step measures test exactly this. This gives a principled reading of L3: narrow bandwidth should give the smallest, not the largest, per-pass Jacobian at stored states. GeGLU's radius of about 3.3 with relative step 1.47 is the signature of a non-mode-seeking, expanding map.

candidates.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 3.1, Knowledge Storage and Extraction (Allen-Zhu, Li)
candidates.why: Synthetic-biography setup that our seen/held-out template measure mirrors. Knowledge becomes extractable in unseen formats only when pretraining data is augmented (paraphrases, shuffles). Without augmentation the model memorizes but extraction can be 0%. Probing shows the cause: extractable facts are linearly encoded on the entity-name tokens, while memorized facts are spread over the template tokens. For L4 and L5, this suggests a mechanistic check beyond accuracy: probe whether looping moves attribute information onto the name tokens (wording-invariant, L5 for Cos T = 2) or deepens template-specific storage (a wider seen/held-out gap, L4 for Cos T = 1 with AdamW).

candidates.title: Stabilizing Equilibrium Models by Jacobian Regularization
candidates.why: ICML 2021 (Bai, Koltun, Kolter). The spectral radius of the Jacobian at equilibrium directly controls forward and backward convergence. In unregularized DEQs on WikiText-103, the radius grows during training and then 'explodes', with perplexity following. A Hutchinson estimate of ||J||_F only upper-bounds the radius, but penalizing it does constrain the radius. Bearing for L3 and our per-pass spectral radius, spectral norm and |J-I|: they suggest a control arm, a Jacobian-penalized GeGLU. That would separate 'narrow kernel makes passes contractive or expansive' from 'any contractive FFN cleans up'. Caveat: their Jacobian is of f at a fixed point z = f(z); ours is I + J_f of a residual update.

candidates.title: Path Independent Equilibrium Models Can Better Exploit Test-Time Computation
candidates.why: NeurIPS 2022 (Anil et al.). Defines path independence as reaching the same steady state from any initialization. It correlates with gains from more test-time iterations ('upwards generalization'). Interventions that promote it help, and those that penalize it hurt. Bearing: our measure of accuracy under relative state noise of 0.1/0.25/0.5 is in effect a path-independence probe, so L2 is a path-independence claim. The paper predicts that only path-independent models (Cos-Bochner, if L2 holds) should gain at K_test=8 > K_train. Expansive GeGLU (radius about 3.3) should not.

candidates.title: Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning: A Recurrent Depth Approach
candidates.why: Recurrent-depth LM (Huginn, 3.5B parameters, 800B tokens). The authors state the recurrent model 'has less capacity to memorize facts but more capacity to reason about its context'. Knowledge-light or easy tasks such as OpenBookQA saturate within a few recurrences, while GSM8k keeps improving. Training samples a random recurrence count per sequence (log-normal Poisson, with backpropagation through only the last 8 steps). That is what makes test-time unrolling work. Tokens converge to fixed points, or to orbits on hard inputs, from different initial states. Bearing: this is a further prior that recall gains from looping (L1) will be small. It also explains why our fixed-K training is not expected to extrapolate to K_test=8. The fixed-point-versus-orbit view gives a way to read our per-pass relative step.

candidates.title: Overparameterized Neural Networks Implement Associative Memory
candidates.why: Radhakrishnan, Belkin and Uhler (PNAS 2020). Overparameterized autoencoders trained with standard optimizers store their training samples as attractors, and repeatedly applying the learned map recovers them. Bearing: this is the mechanism L2 relies on, where iterating a trained map cleans noisy states up toward stored ones. It also gives the test: the per-pass Jacobian at stored states should be contractive (radius below 1). Caveat: their maps are trained as autoencoders that fix the samples. Our FFN is trained for task loss at a fixed K with a=1, so attracting stored states are not guaranteed, and GeGLU's expanding map shows they are absent there.

candidates.title: Energy Transformer (Hoover et al.)
candidates.why: A weight-tied recurrent transformer whose blocks descend an engineered energy. Its Hopfield module is an MLP applied recurrently in which the down-projection is the transpose of the up-projection (xi^T r(xi g)). The proof that energy decreases is continuous-time and relies on this symmetric structure. Discrete runs use a small step (alpha = 0.1, described as giving a smoother descent). Our looped FFN has an independent W_o and step a = 1, so it has no Lyapunov function, and neither GeGLU nor Cos-Bochner is guaranteed to clean up (L2). This suggests two controls: measure the alignment of W_o with W^T (or with the stored-state directions), and rerun the loop at a = 0.1-0.25 to separate step-size blow-up from the absence of an attractor.

candidates.title: Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories (Geva, Schuster, Berant, Levy)
candidates.why: FFN keys detect input patterns and values promote output-vocabulary directions. The layer output is a composition of memories that the residual stream refines. In our facts model, the last FFN's values write attribute directions, a hetero-associative map, so each tied pass re-adds roughly the same value instead of pulling h back toward a stored key. This fits GeGLU's expanding per-pass Jacobian and the slight drop in accuracy with K (0.938 / 0.933 / 0.926), and it argues against L1 and L2 unless Cos-Bochner learns values that point back toward the keys. Suggested diagnostic: the cosine between f(LN(h_k)) and f(LN(h_{k+1})) across passes.

candidates.title: Understanding Factual Recall in Transformers via Associative Memories (Nichani, Lee, Bietti)
candidates.why: arXiv preprint. Proves that the storage capacity of linear and MLP associative memories scales linearly with parameter count. A one-layer attention plus MLP transformer reaches 100% factual recall when either the attention or the MLP parameters scale (up to log factors) linearly with the number of facts. Weight-tied looping adds no parameters, so it cannot raise the storage ceiling for 8192 x 4 facts in a width-128 model. Any L1 gain must come from better separation or denoising at retrieval, not from more storage. Computing facts per FFN parameter for each arm tells whether GeGLU at 0.93 is capacity-limited, which bounds how much looping could ever add.

candidates.title: Adaptive Loops and Memory in Transformers: Think Harder or Know More?
candidates.why: Practitioner-scale preprint (Frey et al.): a 12-layer model of about 200M parameters trained on 14B FineWeb-Edu tokens, with adaptive per-layer looping up to 3, 5 or 7 iterations. Loop-3 cuts math bits-per-byte from 2.163 to 1.687, but commonsense accuracy only moves from 0.477 to 0.501 and then drifts down with more loops (0.498 at Loop-7). Gated memory banks, not loops, recover the commonsense gap: 'looping ... cannot compensate for insufficient storage capacities.' They also use learnable per-step loop scales initialized near identity for stability, unlike our a=1. Bearing: a further independent 'looping does not add storage' data point against a general L1 effect. The scale-near-identity trick is a cheap fix if GeGLU's expansive passes are what hurt it.

candidates.title: Associative Retrieval as Test-Time Optimization in Transformer Attention
candidates.why: Obscure ICLR 2026 NFAM workshop poster (Roy and Roy; a preliminary study on synthetic Gaussian vectors and MNIST embeddings). Repeatedly applying attention, an exponential-kernel smoother over stored keys, improves retrieval from partial or noisy cues by 13-16%, with stable, attractor-like convergence. Bearing: this is the nearest direct analog of L2 for a kernel smoother. Cos-Bochner approximates a Gaussian kernel smoother, so iterating it is mean-shift or Hopfield-like and could clean up in a way GeGLU does not. It also gives a rough expected effect size. Weak evidence: small scale and not peer-reviewed.

candidates.title: Resonator Networks outperform optimization methods at solving high-dimensional vector factorization (Kent, Frady, Sommer, Olshausen; Resonator Networks part 2)
candidates.why: Long-form preprint (Neural Computation 2020) from the vector-symbolic / hyperdimensional computing literature on iterated codebook clean-up. Unlike Hopfield networks, resonator dynamics have no known Lyapunov function. Trajectories can fall into limit cycles or seemingly chaotic orbits, yet they almost always converge inside an 'operational capacity' regime that scales quadratically with dimension. This is the right null for running past the trained K (K_test = 8): in an iterated clean-up map without an energy, expect convergence inside a load-dependent capacity regime and oscillation or drift outside it. Check the per-pass relative step for period-2 patterns, and compare the load (facts per dimension) across arms when judging L1 and L2.

reads.title: Scaling Latent Reasoning via Looped Language Models (Ouro), arXiv 2510.25741 (v6, 11 Oct 2026)
reads.sections_read: Read the full v6 PDF (54 pages). There is no arXiv HTML for the unversioned ID. Covered: Abstract; Sec. 1-2; Sec. 3 (architecture, exit gate, entropy-regularized Stage I, Stage II adaptive gate); Sec. 4 (recipe, Table 1, stability notes, SFT, RL attempts); Sec. 5 (base and Thinking evals, Tables 10-13 depth extrapolation, early exit, KV sharing); Sec. 6.1-6.3 (Capo capacity, Mano, multi-hop QA, reachability theorem); Sec. 7 (safety, faithfulness and step agreement, deployment); Sec. 8; App. A (prior ablation); App. B.1-B.5 (Capo details and capacity definition, Mano, multi-hop QA plus extra figures, MMLU per-category Table 15, theorem and proof); App. C (eval settings); App. D.1-D.3 and E.1-E.2 (loop scaling laws). I rendered Figures 6 and 7 at high resolution and read values off them. Other figures were read from their captions and the extracted tick text.
reads.setup: Main models: Ouro 1.4B (24 layers) and 2.6B (48 layers, made by duplicating the 24 layers). Both are decoder-only, MHA + RoPE, SwiGLU FFN, pre-RMSNorm before attention and FFN. The whole layer stack is looped with weights tied across passes. Training: 7.7T tokens with AdamW (0.9, 0.95), wd 0.1, clip 1.0. Stage 1a (3T tokens) used 8 recurrent steps. Stages 1b-4 used 4 steps. Every step has an LM head. The loss is the expected per-step loss under a learned exit distribution p(t|x) minus beta times its entropy (uniform prior; beta 0.1 then 0.05), so steps 1..T_max are all supervised (deep supervision). Stage II then trains only the exit gate on loss-improvement labels. Section 6 synthetic tests use GPT-2 with RoPE and tied embeddings (notation a-b-lc: 64a hidden, b layers, c loops of the whole stack). (1) Capo knowledge capacity: bioS(N) synthetic biographies, N = 20K/50K/100K/200K/500K, 1000 exposures, lr 1e-3, wd 0.02, batch 192, context 512; models of 1M-40M params; loop-1 vs loop-4 at equal parameters. Capacity is measured in bits from the summed attribute-token cross-entropy, with partial credit (Allen-Zhu Def.); log2 S0 is about 47.6 bits per person plus name bits. (2) Mano: modular-arithmetic trees mod 23, hidden 1024, base {2,3,6,12}x1 vs loops k x 12/k, LR swept over 4 values, best of 3 seeds. (3) 3-hop QA (Yao et al.): 6 layers, 1024 wide, loops {1,2,4}, 20K steps, batch 2048, 4 seeds averaged, 3000 held-out questions, an iso-FLOP 24x1 baseline. Appendix D: loop scaling laws at 53M-1.36B, 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, T_max in {1,2,4,8}.
key_results: Capacity (Sec. 6.1, Fig. 6 left): GPT-2, 1M-40M params, bioS N = 20K-500K, 1000 exposures. Loop-1 and loop-4 at equal parameters both sit near the 2 bits/param line. The paper states that 'looping does not increase knowledge capacity nor improve capacity scaling'. These values come only from a log-log scatter: there is no table, no seed count and no error bars.

In Fig. 6 left most points are data-saturated. Each N forms a flat row across model sizes: about 1.3e6 bits (20K), 3.3e6 (50K), 6.5e6 (100K), 1.3e7 (200K) and 3.1e7 (500K). Only the few smallest models in each row (about 1M-15M params) are capacity-limited, so only they can separate loop from no-loop. The loop-1 and loop-4 markers differ only by size and sit on top of each other.

Mano (Fig. 6 right; exact match at the hardest length L = 10/16/24; best of 3 seeds): Base 2x1 21.5/8.4/7.5 vs Loop 2x6 98.1/96.3/78.0. Base 3x1 75.4/29.8/11.0 vs Loop 3x4 97.9/95.8/92.2. Base 6x1 84.7/59.5/20.0 vs Loop 6x2 93.4/88.5/35.1. The iso-FLOP Base 12x1 scores 93.6/94.4/34.8.

3-hop QA (Fig. 7; 6 layers, 1024 wide, 20K steps, 4-seed average): at 120K unique training pairs (15%), the right panel ends at about 62% (loop 4), 33% (loop 2) and 14% (loop 1). The left panel gives about 51/26/17% for the same 120K. Loop 4 reaches 100% at 140K unique pairs, loop 2 at 160K, and loop 1 is still at about 86% at 200K. Against the iso-FLOP 24x1 model the evidence is mixed: loop 2 is below it at 100K (Fig. 12), and footnote 5 says the iso-FLOP model at 120K was not better than the shallower model, possibly from randomness or tuning.

Depth extrapolation, base models (Tables 10-11; nominally trained at T = 4). 1.4B MMLU: 41.21 (T=1), 60.43, 66.71, 67.45 (T=4), 66.64 (T=5), 64.49 (T=8). 1.4B ARC-C: 60.92 (T=4) to 58.19 (T=8). 2.6B MMLU: 74.60 to 72.24. 2.6B HellaSwag: 79.56 to 79.50 (flat).

Depth extrapolation, Thinking/SFT models (Tables 12-13), which degrade much more. 2.6B OlympiadBench: 76.44 (T=4) to 39.26 (T=8). 2.6B AIME24: 64.70 to 39.00. 2.6B AIME25: 50.30 to 24.33. 1.4B AIME24: 65.00 to 38.67. The 1.4B Thinking model peaks at T = 4-5 and the 2.6B at T = 3-4.

Stability (Sec. 4.3): 8 recurrent steps in Stage 1a 'led to loss spikes and gradient oscillations'. The cause is hypothesized as compounded gradient flow amplifying perturbations, but no curves are shown. The fix changed several things together: steps 8 to 4, batch 4M to 8M, beta 0.1 to 0.05. The paper also says recurrent models need smaller LRs than parameter-matched transformers, without a sweep. The App. D runs at T_max = 8 (up to 1.36B, 20B tokens) report no instability.

Untied deeper ('Standard', more params) vs LoopLM at the same step count (App. D.1, Table 18): Standard is better in every case, and the gap grows with steps. At 170M the average benchmark gap is 0.021 at step 2 and 0.039 at step 4; at 1.3B it is 0.017 and 0.025. For the 778M and 1.36B LoopLMs, more recurrent steps (up to 8) did not raise benchmark scores (Fig. 14).

App. D.3: in small models, the shallow-step losses rise as training data grows, because the gate shifts weight to deep steps. In the T_max = 4 scaling-law runs the learned exit weights on MMLU are about {0.0004, 0.0855, 0.3793, 0.5348} for t = 1..4.

MMLU per category (App. B.4; T=1 vs T=4 readouts of the same T=4-trained 1.4B model). Small gains: global_facts 0.36 to 0.39 (+8.3%), virology 0.44 to 0.50 (+13.7%), anatomy 0.41 to 0.50 (+21.4%), moral_scenarios 0.24 to 0.26 (+7.8%). Large gains: elementary_math 0.31 to 0.79 (+156%). But knowledge-heavy categories also roughly doubled: hs_psychology 0.418 to 0.839 (+100%), hs_biology 0.413 to 0.816 (+98%), clinical_knowledge 0.415 to 0.694 (+67%).

Step-to-step agreement (Sec. 7.2; Quora Question Pairs, 1,000 items, 1.4B): A[2,3] = 551, A[3,4] = 788, A[2,4] = 361. Beyond the trained depth: A[4,5] = 922, A[5,6] = 932, A[6,7] = 927, A[7,8] = 928. Predictions change less per step past T = 4, which the authors read as approach to a fixed point; no state-space measure is given. The hidden-state-difference exit (||h_t - h_{t-1}|| < eps) comes within 1-2% MMLU accuracy of the trained gate at 2-3 average rounds.

Theorem 2 (App. B.5): a 1-layer looped transformer of width 2n, with full attention and a Boolean threshold in place of LayerNorm, solves reachability on a hidden-plus-context graph in 1 + ceil(log2 max(1, D)) loops. The authors say themselves that this does not cover causal attention or standard normalization and does not explain the empirical gaps.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L1: looping helps narrow Cos-Bochner more than GeGLU on recall
bearing_on_predictions.reason: Ouro's null is about storage capacity at saturation: whole-stack looping of GPT-2 GeLU-MLP blocks, 1000 exposures, measured in loss-based bits. Our facts runs are not in that regime. The GeGLU model has 608,928 trainable params and the Cos width-16,384 model 4,407,968 (computed from rcdl/facts.py). The task holds 8,192 x 4 x 5 = 163,840 bits, which is 0.27 bits/param (GeGLU) and 0.037 (Cos), far below 2. Training gives about 39 exposures per fact (10,000 x 128 / 32,768). So recall here is limited by learning speed or optimization, not capacity. In that regime Ouro's only loop effects are faster learning of composition tasks (multi-hop QA, Mano). GeGLU's 0.938/0.933/0.926 has the same sign as Ouro's null, but it is not evidence of a capacity null. It could also be optimization: the per-pass map is expanding (radius about 3.3, relative step 1.47), and Ouro reports that recurrent models need smaller LRs. Ouro has no data on kernel FFNs. A Cos gain would not contradict it; it would point to retrieval or clean-up, which Ouro would file under 'manipulation', not storage.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L2: looping improves noise robustness (clean-up toward stored states) more for Cos-Bochner
bearing_on_predictions.reason: There is no noise or perturbation test. The indirect hints cut both ways. Pass-to-pass label agreement rises past the trained depth (A[i,i+1] about 922-932 for i >= 4), and ||h_t - h_{t-1}|| works as an exit signal, so iterates slow down. But base-model accuracy falls past T = 4 (1.4B MMLU 67.45 to 64.49 at T = 8), so the slowing is not convergence onto correct states, i.e. not demonstrated clean-up. Nothing compares FFN types.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L3: the narrow kernel has the largest per-pass Jacobian
bearing_on_predictions.reason: There are no Jacobian, spectral or contraction measurements. The paper only hypothesizes, without measuring, that the 8-step loss spikes come from compounded gradient flow amplifying small perturbations. That makes per-pass expansion worth measuring and suggests expanding maps hurt more as K grows, but it gives no data on any kernel.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L4: looping widens Cos-Bochner T = 1's seen/held-out gap
bearing_on_predictions.reason: Ouro never tests held-out wording. Capacity is measured on the training biographies themselves, and the bioS template regime is unclear ('a random selected fixed template'). Its only held-out test is multi-hop QA, where looping improves generalization to unseen compositions at a fixed unique-sample budget. Its Sec. 6.3 conjecture is that tying shrinks the hypothesis class and so improves sample efficiency. Both lean toward looping closing generalization gaps, not widening them, but paraphrase invariance is a different axis. The 'reallocation of fixed storage' reading also fits poorly here. Our bios GeGLU model has 6.13M params and the facts amount to about 8,192 x 59 bits, roughly 0.08 bits/param at about 236 exposures per individual (322 bios/step x 6,000 steps). Storage is not binding, so a wider gap would more likely come from the inductive bias of iterating a narrow kernel than from capacity.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L5: Cos T = 2 stays wording-invariant under looping
bearing_on_predictions.reason: There is nothing on template invariance. The extrapolation results imply that L5 should be judged at K_test = K_train and separately at K_test > K_train. Even a wording-invariant model may lose accuracy at K_test = 8 for reasons unrelated to wording.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: Working assumption: K_test = 8 > K_train will degrade
bearing_on_predictions.reason: Base models lose about 2-3 points by T = 8 (1.4B MMLU 67.45 to 64.49; 2.6B 74.60 to 72.24), and Thinking models lose up to half (2.6B OlympiadBench 76.44 to 39.26). Two caveats make our case likely worse. Ouro supervises every step 1..4 through the exit distribution, while our models get a loss only at pass K. And Ouro's T = 5-8 is not pure extrapolation, because Stage 1a (3T tokens) trained at 8 steps.

critical_gaps: The 'no capacity gain' claim rests on one log-log scatter with no table, no seeds and no error bars, with overlapping loop-1/loop-4 markers. Most points sit on data-saturated rows where the two cannot differ. Only about 10-15 small-model points test capacity, and a 10-20% difference would be hard to see on a log axis.

The Capo configuration is under-specified. The paper does not say which a-b sizes were run, whether loop and no-loop pairs share a-b, or whether looped models were trained with final-step loss or the gated multi-step objective. One LR (1e-3) was used for both, although Sec. 4.3 says recurrent models need smaller LRs. Under-tuned looped models could hide a gain.

The dataset description is inconsistent. The text says five attributes, but S0 = 2 x (12*28*200) x 200 x 300 x 100 x 263 has six factors (gender, birth date, city, university, major, employer). Sec. 6.1 lists gender and B.1 lists city of birth. 'Online sample the individual attributes' is ambiguous given fixed facts. Whether templates are single and fixed or random per exposure is unclear, and that matters for Allen-Zhu's capacity numbers.

Capacity is measured only at 1000 exposures, i.e. saturation. Nothing is said about few-exposure learning speed, the regime where looping helped multi-hop QA and where our runs sit (about 39 facts exposures, about 236 bios exposures).

Only whole-stack looping of GPT-2 GeLU-MLP blocks is tested. There is no single-FFN looping, no gated or kernel FFN, and no knowledge-extraction or held-out-template evaluation, so the paper says nothing about wording invariance or FFN-type interactions.

The 'storage vs manipulation' MMLU analysis compares T=1 and T=4 readouts of one T=4-trained model, where step 1 probably gets near-zero exit weight. Relative percentages inflate low baselines, and near-chance categories (global_facts 0.36-0.39, moral_scenarios 0.24-0.26) cannot move. Several knowledge-heavy categories roughly doubled (hs_psychology +100%, hs_biology +98%). The split is post hoc, so 'gains only in manipulation' is too strong.

Mano reports the best of 3 seeds. The iso-FLOP 12x1 model falls to 34.8 at L = 24 while 3x4 reaches 92.2, which may reflect how hard a deeper untied net is to optimize at a fixed budget rather than looping's inductive bias. App. B.2 also confuses expression length L with 'model depths L in {10,16,24}'.

The multi-hop iso-FLOP comparison is mixed, and footnote 5 admits it may be under-tuned. 'Same compute budget in training tokens' is not iso-FLOP. The two Fig. 7 panels disagree for the same 120K condition (about 51/26/17% vs 62/33/14%).

'Trained with a maximum of 4 steps' is inaccurate: Stage 1a ran 3T tokens at 8 steps, so T = 5-8 was seen during training. All of steps 1-4 are also supervised. Neither condition matches final-step-only looping.
The 8-step instability claim is anecdotal. Several settings changed at once, no loss curves are shown, and the scaling-law runs at T_max = 8 report no instability.

The headline 2-3x parameter efficiency compares models trained on different data (Ouro's mid-training includes Q/CoT/A samples and heavy math). There is no same-data non-looped baseline at scale, and App. D shows untied deeper models beat LoopLM at equal step counts.

Safety 'improving' with steps up to T = 8 coincides with falling benchmark accuracy past T = 4 and may reflect lost capability. The faithfulness analysis is observational (probes, agreement), not causal.
App. D model sizes are inconsistent: Table 18 lists 170M/340M/680M/1.3B, but the text lists 53M/134M/374M/778M/1.36B.
measures_we_lack: Loss-based bits of knowledge with partial credit (Ouro/Allen-Zhu Def. 1) per trainable parameter, alongside top-1 accuracy, for each FFN and K. Report Cos's fixed W separately. Add an N sweep (e.g. 8K to 64K+ individuals) or narrower models until GeGLU at K = 1 saturates. Ouro's null applies only there; currently we are at 0.27 (GeGLU) and 0.037 (Cos) bits per trainable param.

Exposure control and learning curves: accuracy and bits vs step for each K, plus either training to saturation or matching exposures. This separates 'faster learning' (Ouro's multi-hop-type effect) from 'more storage'. Facts are now at about 39 exposures and bios at about 236.

An iso-FLOP untied control: K separately parameterized FFN copies (Cos copies with independent random W), next to the iso-param K = 1 baseline. This is Ouro's 12x1 / 24x1 role and separates 'extra compute' from 'weight tying'.

Per-pass readout: apply ln_f and the head after every pass and report per-pass accuracy and pass-to-pass prediction agreement (Ouro's A[i,j]) up to K_test = 8 (or 16). This shows convergence vs drift beyond K_train.

Dynamics beyond the trained depth. loop_probe in /home/user/rcdltesting/rcdl/facts.py iterates `for k in range(model.cfg.loops)`, so Jacobian radius, norm, |J - I| and relative step are recorded only for passes 1..K_train and are missing for the K_test = 8 passes. Extend it to every pass up to 8, and log ||h_k - h_{k-1}|| as Ouro's exit signal does.
A deep-supervision or random-K variant (loss at every pass, or K sampled per step), so that K_test != K_train is compared fairly with Ouro's regime.

LR and stability controls per K. Facts uses Adam lr 1e-3 with no gradient clipping at every K, and GeGLU's per-pass map is expanding (radius about 3.3). Log gradient norms and loss spikes, and run at least one lower LR at K = 4, so the slight GeGLU decline is not an optimization artifact.
More seeds with mean and range reported, never best-of. We run 2 seeds, and identical Cos bios runs have differed by 9 points.
For L4: bits (not only accuracy) on seen and held-out templates, so wording memorization and fact storage can be compared in the same units.

Optional: a 2-hop facts query (attribute of the individual named by another attribute). This tests whether kernel looping helps where Ouro finds looping helps, i.e. composition rather than single-hop recall.

reads.title: Reasoning with Latent Thoughts: On the Power of Looped Transformers (Saunshi, Dikkala, Li, Kumar, Reddi; Google Research; ICLR 2025)
reads.sections_read: I read the whole arXiv HTML of v1, the only version (24 Feb 2025), saved at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-rcdltesting/67502866-e3ee-5513-b270-94b7a7c21d08/scratchpad/paper/p.txt. That covers the abstract, Sections 1-7, the references, Appendix A.1-A.3 (setup details and the per-task Tables 5-8) and Appendix B.1-B.3 (notation and the proofs of Thm 5.1, 5.2 and B.5 with Lemmas B.1-B.11). I also opened the figure images and read values off them: Fig 2 (12L and 24L isoplots for closed-book QA, open-book QA, math word problems and primitives), all six panels of Fig 3 (depth scaling, with the alpha_loop/alpha_base values in the panel titles) and the closed-book and open-book panels of Fig 7 (8L). For Figs 1, 4, 5 and 6 (the cosine-similarity heatmaps) I read only the captions.
key_results: LM, Table 3 (Pile, single seed). The 24-layer baseline scores perplexity 7.40, closed-book 11.2, open-book 33.9, math word problems 29.3, primitives 47.5. (12⊗2) against iso-param (12⊗1): perplexity 7.90 vs 8.16, closed-book 9.3 vs 8.2, open-book 30.8 vs 26.9, math 34.3 vs 26.7, primitives 51.2 vs 35.7.

%Gap, Table 3, in the order perplexity / closed-book / open-book / math / primitives: k=12: 34/37/56/282/131; k=8: 41/44/72/92/153; k=6: 44/58/64/104/136; k=4: 48/52/61/77/133. Middle loop (4⊗1,4,1), iso-param with 12 layers: 46/94/78/62/176, with closed-book 11.0 against the 24-layer model's 11.2. So 'closed-book %Gap ≈ perplexity %Gap' holds within 3-14 points for plain looping and fails for middle looping.
Looping raises closed-book QA over the iso-param model in every case: k=4 1.8→6.7, k=6 4.0→8.2, k=8 6.3→8.5, k=12 8.2→9.3. It still falls short of the 24-layer model's 11.2.

Depth scaling (Fig 3, (4⊗D/4) vs (D⊗1), D up to 48), α_loop/α_base: perplexity 0.5, token accuracy 0.5, closed-book 0.5, open-book 0.6, math 0.6, primitives 1.2 (text: 1.19). Read from the figure: looped closed-book is about 1.8 at D=4, 8.4 at D=36 and 7.8 at D=48 (falls at 12 loops); the D=48 baseline is about 15.2.

Isoplots (Fig 2 and 7). Closed-book lines of (12⊗2) vs (12⊗1) and (8⊗3) vs (8⊗1) line up only when extrapolated: the perplexity ranges barely overlap (12L) or do not overlap (8L), with about 6 checkpoints per run. For open-book and primitives, the looped line sits above the baseline at the same log-perplexity: about +3 points open-book and +15 primitives for 12L. The primitives lines are flat, so this is a level shift present from step 120k on.

Primitives per task (Table 8): the gain comes almost entirely from depth-0 variable lookup. (4⊗6) code/math depth-0 is 87.9/90.0 against the 24-layer model's 71.1/72.5; depth-1 is 24.8/24.8 against 24.2/22.3. Math word problems are low throughout; MultiArith is 0.7-3.5% for every model.

Regularizer (Table 4, 24 layers, single seed). Perplexity 7.38-7.51 against 7.40. Closed-book: 11.2 (k=4, λ=1), 12.5 (k=4, λ=10), 12.0 (k=6), 11.3 (k=8), 10.1 (k=12), against 11.2. Open-book 34.1-36.2 against 33.9; math 31.0-36.4 against 29.3; primitives 42.5 (k=4, λ=1, below the baseline) to 57.2. Cosine similarity between blocks is about ≥0.98 at λ=10.

The regularizer's closed-book isoplot (Fig 2, bottom left; k=4, λ=10) lies about 0.5-1 point above the baseline at equal log-perplexity, although the text calls the plots 'similar'. For k=4, λ=10 the relative closed-book gain (+12%: 11.2→12.5) is larger than the relative open-book gain (+7%: 33.9→36.2).

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L1: looping helps narrow Cos-Bochner more than GeGLU on recall
bearing_on_predictions.reason: This is a weak prior, and narrower than the usual summary. The paper does not show that looping fails to help recall. Looping raised closed-book QA over the iso-param model in all four budgets (e.g. 1.8→6.7 at k=4). The claim is that the gain is proportionate: closed-book %Gap tracks perplexity %Gap (37-58% vs 34-48%), and α_loop/α_base is 0.5 for both. So looping lifts recall only as far as it lifts the loss, with no extra recall benefit. The paper has one FFN type, so it says nothing about the FFN-type × looping interaction L1 is about. It also loops whole attention+FFN blocks, while we loop only the last FFN. Our early GeGLU numbers (0.938/0.933/0.926 for K=1/2/4) fall with K, whereas the paper's looped models gain over iso-param. That is consistent with FFN-only looping at the readout adding no capacity, and it gives L1 nothing to amplify unless Cos-Bochner's iteration does something qualitatively different, such as clean-up. One counterweight: middle looping reached 94% closed-book %Gap (11.0 vs 11.2), so loop placement can move recall a lot. Our loop sits directly before the readout.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L2: looping improves noise robustness (clean-up toward stored states) more for Cos-Bochner
bearing_on_predictions.reason: The paper has no noise injection, no fixed-point or attractor analysis and no test-time loop variation. Its 'latent thoughts' account treats loops as computation steps, not as convergence to stored states. It offers no evidence either way.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L3: the narrow kernel has the largest per-pass Jacobian
bearing_on_predictions.reason: The paper reports no Jacobian, norm-growth or step-size measures. Its theory uses hand-built constructions with exact gating, so it says nothing about the Lipschitz behaviour of learned loops.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L4: looping widens Cos-Bochner T=1's seen/held-out gap
bearing_on_predictions.reason: The paper's only bias claim runs the other way. At equal loss, looping (and the tied-block regularizer) improves tasks that use the context: open-book QA and depth-0 variable lookup. Closed-book knowledge tracks the loss. Nothing in it suggests looping favours surface memorization of wording, and better parsing of new wording would, if anything, narrow the gap. Two caveats weaken this. First, the effect the paper credits plausibly runs through looped attention, and in our bios task attention runs once and only the last FFN loops. Second, the paper's 'memorization' (closed-book QA learned from diverse text) is closer to our held-out-template knowledge than to verbatim wording. Its prediction is therefore that any change in the gap under looping is explained by the change in training loss, which an isoplot can check.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L5: Cos T=2 stays wording-invariant under looping
bearing_on_predictions.reason: This is weak, indirect support. Closed-book isoplots of looped and unlooped models roughly coincide, and the k=4 regularizer even sits slightly above the baseline. So in the paper, tying or looping did not degrade how stored knowledge is expressed at a given loss, which fits looping leaving a wording-invariant solution intact. The paper has no wording-invariance or template-generalization test, single seeds and ≤6 checkpoints per fit, so this is only a weak prior.

critical_gaps: The headline 'closed-book %Gap equals perplexity %Gap' is approximate: the two differ by 3, 3, 14 and 4 points across k=12/8/6/4. It fails outright for middle looping (94% vs 46%). The paper explains that case only as 'more uniform improvements', which undercuts 'memorization depends on parameter count'.

'Memorization depends on parameter count' is inferred, never tested. There is no capacity-controlled synthetic recall task and no bits-per-parameter measure, and every synthetic task was built so that memorization is impossible. Closed-book QA after Pile pretraining mixes storage with extracting knowledge from varied text and with question parsing.

The 'disproportionate reasoning' effect is thin outside the primitives. In the scaling fits, open-book and math have α_loop/α_base of 0.6 against 0.5 for closed-book and perplexity, with no confidence intervals and only 6 depths. Primitives (1.2) are the only clear case.

The primitives gain is almost all depth-0 lookup (e.g. 87.9/90.0 vs 71.1/72.5); depth-1 barely moves (24.8 vs 24.2/22.3). Open-book QA is also in-context retrieval. The bias the data actually show could be toward retrieval from the context rather than toward multi-step reasoning, so 'reasoning vs memorization' may really be 'reading from context vs reading from weights'.

All LM results are single seed with no error bars. Absolute scores are tiny: closed-book 1.8-12.5%, NQ 0.6-4.5%, MultiArith 0.7-3.5%. %Gap is unstable when its denominator is small (math 282% at k=12 comes from a 2.6-point baseline gap). The synthetic tasks report the best of 3 seeds, which favours whichever arm has the higher variance.

The learning rate was tuned on the 24-layer baseline and reused for looped and shallow models. Looped models may be under-tuned, so part of their perplexity and recall deficit could be optimization rather than capacity.

The isoplots fit about 6 correlated checkpoints from one run each, confounded with the phase of the cosine LR schedule. The closed-book alignment needs extrapolation because the perplexity ranges barely overlap (12L) or do not overlap (8L). The regularized-vs-baseline closed-book isoplot shows an offset of about +1 point, yet the text calls it similar.

The regularizer does not leave closed-book QA neatly unchanged: it ranges from −1.1 (k=12) to +1.3 (k=4, λ=10), and at k=4, λ=10 the relative closed-book gain (+12%) exceeds the open-book gain (+7%). λ=1 lowers primitives to 42.5 from 47.5. So the 'dichotomy' under regularization is not cleanly shown.

The paper does not look at internal dynamics. There are no per-loop representation changes, Jacobians, fixed points, norm growth, robustness to perturbation or evaluation at loop counts other than the trained one. Looped models get worse past 9 loops (closed-book 8.4→7.8 and math 27→26 from D=36 to D=48), and this is not explained.

Only whole-block looping and a single FFN type are tested, with no FFN-only looping. The theory consists of existence constructions with exact weights (ReLU gates, finite precision) and makes no claims about learnability or memory capacity.

Reporting inconsistencies: the model is called 1B in the text and 1.5B in A.2. The first open-book column of Table 6 is labelled 'TydiQA-NoContext' but presumably holds GoldP, since its values (33.4) differ from the closed-book TydiQA-NoContext (10.6).
measures_we_lack: An untied iso-FLOP arm. Add K distinct last-FFN blocks; for Cos-Bochner in the facts task, K independent random feature maps W, b with K trained W_o. With it we can compute the paper's %Gap = (acc_loop_K − acc_K1)/(acc_untied_K − acc_K1) per FFN type and state L1 as an interaction on %Gap or on α_loop/α_base, not on raw accuracy. This also corrects for headroom: GeGLU sits at 0.938, and Cos-Bochner may be near the ceiling.

Isoplots. Log training loss together with facts recall, and with bios seen and held-out accuracy, at each eval step (eval_every is 500 for facts and 100 for bios), then compare the metric-vs-loss lines across K. This shows whether looping changes the loss-to-metric relation (a bias) or only the loss. L4 and L5 in particular should be tested at matched training loss.

Fit Acc = α log K + β per FFN type and kernel width, with seed confidence intervals on α and on the Cos-minus-GeGLU difference in α. Two seeds per cell is thin: bios Cos-Bochner seeds already differed by 9 points, and the paper's single-seed and best-of-3 practice shows how easily such effects get overstated.

A loop-placement control. The paper's middle loop moved closed-book %Gap from 37% to 94% at the same parameters and FLOPs. Our loop sits directly before LN_f and the head (end looping). Add an arm that loops an earlier FFN, or that keeps a distinct final FFN after the looped one.

A whole-block looping arm (attention plus FFN), since the paper's effects come from looping whole blocks. In facts.py the last FFN runs only at the last position, so our looping iterates a single-token map with no access to context; in bios.py attention runs once.

Control for trainable-parameter count across FFN types. In the facts task, GeGLU at width 512 has about 197k trainable FFN parameters, while Cos-Bochner at width 16,384 has about 2.1M (W_o only). The paper's central claim is that recall tracks parameter count, so K=1 differences between types confound comparisons of the looping gain unless the gain is normalized as above or parameters are matched.
A soft-tie arm: K untied blocks trained with the paper's cosine-similarity regularizer between blocks. It separates the effect of weight tying from that of added depth.

A positive control for the paper's bias in our setting: a bios or facts variant whose answer must be read from context (open-book style, like depth-0 variable assignment). It tells us whether FFN-only looping can show the reported bias at all.

Per-item breakdowns (per attribute, per template, per kernel width), as in the paper's Tables 5-8, so that an average does not hide an effect concentrated in one subset. The paper's own primitives gain turned out to be depth-0 only.

reads.title: Stability and Generalization in Looped Transformers (Asher Labovich, arXiv 2604.15259v2, 22 Apr 2026)
reads.sections_read: Read the full arXiv HTML (v2): Abstract; Sections 1-6 (Introduction, Related Work, Preliminaries with Definitions 3.1-3.4 and the three axes, Section 4 on autonomous networks with Props 1-3, Section 5 on recall networks with Props 4-5, Conclusion); Appendix A.1-A.8 (all proofs: transversality, joint fixed points, gradient instability, the three spectral cases, recall stability, Prop 5 proof with Lemma 1, explicit Jacobians, independence from e); Appendix B.1-B.6 (data, training details, compute, anisotropy Table 3, Fig 6 on LR vs rho(W_x), Fig 7 on rho(W_x) vs accuracy, Tables 4-6); references. I looked at all five raster figures (Fig 3, Fig 6 external and internal, Fig 7 val and hard). Figures 1, 2, 4 and 5 are inline TikZ, so I read them from their labels and captions. I also read rcdl/facts.py and the looping parts of rcdl/bios.py to map the theory onto our probes.
reads.setup: Theory plus a small empirical study. The theory treats a looped network as a discrete dynamical system x_{t+1} = f_theta(x_t, ...) on R^{d x L}. It has two forms. In the autonomous form, x_{t+1} = f(x_t). In the recall form, x_{t+1} = f(x_t, x_0), and the recall comes in two placements, external (it replaces the residual input) or internal (it enters only the update). The theory also covers optional outer normalization phi applied to each iterate's output (post-norm or GRU). Success is defined as reaching an input-dependent fixed point, judged on three axes: reachability (rho of the fixed-point Jacobian < 1), input-dependence, and geometry (how isotropic the stable parameter region is). The paper assumes smooth f and a transversality condition. The experiments use a single-layer transformer as the looped block: d = 256, 8 heads (head dim 64), QK-norm, multi-dimensional RoPE (sliding window 5 for prefix sums), GELU MLP of width 1024, RMSNorm everywhere. Looped models have 0.98M params with GRU and 1.39M without; the fixed-depth baselines have 15 layers and 11.9M/17.8M params. The norm sweep is pre / peri / post / GRU. The recall sweep is none (autonomous) / external / internal / fixed-depth, with linear recall g = W_x x_t + W_0 x_0. Three tasks, each with a harder test set: prefix sums (train 32-bit, test 512-bit), sudoku-extreme (train below the 80th-percentile backtrack count, test above it), and Lichess puzzles (train ELO < 1600, test 1600-2000). Training: AdamW (wd 0.01), 100 epochs, batch 500, LR sweep (1e-4/3e-4/1e-3; sudoku 3e-4/1e-3/3e-3), 3 seeds. Every model uses Bansal-style progressive loss with alpha = 1: draw N ~ U[0, 29] passes without gradients, then K ~ U[1, 29-N] passes with gradients, and take the loss only on the final K. Max T = 30 in training; evaluation runs out to 500 iterations in Fig 3. Compute: 120 B200 GPU-hours.
key_results: Prop 1 (smooth f, Assumption 1 that [dg/dx, dg/dtheta] spans the state space, g = f(x) - x): for almost all theta, J_f at any fixed point has no eigenvalue exactly 1.

Prop 2 (same assumptions, autonomous loop): for almost all theta the fixed-point set is a dimension-zero manifold. It is countable, and finite if the state is confined to a compact set as under post-norm. The paper concludes that an autonomous loop's input-dependence reduces to 'basin selection'. Appendix A.2 extends this to 'joint fixed points' of a readout head under an augmented transversality assumption.

Prop 3 / A.4 (autonomous, assuming the state converges exactly to x* by some step K < T): dx_T/dx_0 = J(x*)^{T-K} A(x_0, theta). Three cases: rho < 1 gives input-gradient decay ~ C alpha^{T-K} ('input forgotten'); rho > 1 makes the center-stable manifold of dimension < dL, so the fixed point is 'practically never reached'; rho -> 1 from below makes dx*/dtheta = -(J - I)^{-1} df/dtheta blow up.

Prop 4 (recall, no outer norm): x* is attracting iff rho(M_ext) < 1 with M_ext = (I + J_h2)(I + J_h1) J_g, or iff rho(M_int) < 1 with M_int = (I + J_h2 J_g)(I + J_h1 J_g). In the commuting scalar toy (Fig 5), external is stable iff |(1 + lambda_h) lambda_g| < 1 and internal iff |1 + lambda_g lambda_h| < 1.

Prop 5 (any recall model whose iterates converge to x* with rho(df/dx*) < 1): lim_T dx_T/dx_0 = (I - df/dx*)^{-1} df/dx_0. A.8: the fixed point is then locally independent of the initial iterate e. Nothing in the proposition uses outer normalization; its role is argued only informally.

Table 3 anisotropy toy (2-D Gaussian points projected onto the Fig 5 stability regions, n = 10,000 per sigma, sigma = 0.5-4): median log-range is 4.68-18.13 for internal recall vs 0.89-1.76 for external; median balance is 0.0000-0.0092 internal vs 0.17-0.41 external. This is a toy calculation, not a measurement on trained nets.

Fig 6 (pre/peri averaged, no outer norm): rho(W_x) starts at about 0.6 at initialization in every run and stays about 0.6-0.65 at low LR. At high LR (1e-3) external recall reaches about 3.4 (chess), about 4.6-4.9 (sudoku) and about 1.1-1.2 (prefix sums); internal recall reaches about 0.78, about 2.3 and about 0.8.

Fig 7 (external recall, pre-norm, about 27 runs, 'normalized accuracy' with no stated normalizer): accuracy is 0 at rho(W_x) about 1.5 and 2.7 (prefix sums) and about 6.1 (chess). Sudoku runs at rho about 1.05-1.1 still reach normalized val 0.68-0.75 and hard 0.31-0.45, and a prefix-sums run at rho about 0.87 scores 0. The text's claim of no non-zero accuracy 'when the recall Jacobian substantially exceeds 1' rests on about 3-4 points.

Fig 3 (autonomous nets, best norm+LR config per task chosen by hard accuracy, trained to 30 iterations, evaluated to 500): chess val about 48% / hard about 19%. Prefix sums val about 100% from about 20 iterations, drifting to about 93% between about 100 and 300 iterations, hard 0%. Sudoku val about 37% / hard about 8%. So with alpha = 1 progressive loss there is little overthinking beyond training depth.

Tables 4-5 (3-seed means, exact-match accuracy, no SE), outer norm vs none: best normalized vs best un-normalized hard accuracy is 35.95% (post, internal, 1e-3) vs 23.22% (pre, external, 1e-3) on sudoku, +12.7 pts. On chess it is 42.22% (GRU, external, 1e-3) vs 39.29% (pre, external, 3e-4), +2.9 pts. On prefix sums at LR 1e-3 only GRU (64.67/64.38) and post (31.08/1.09) are non-zero, but at LR 1e-4 pre-norm external also reaches 100.00% hard.

Autonomous ('none' recall) rows: hard accuracy 6.0-17.6% on chess, <= 5.01% on sudoku and <= 0.02% on prefix sums. Val accuracy is sometimes high: 92.77% on prefix sums (GRU, 1e-4), 44.61% on chess, and 22.31% on sudoku (GRU, 3e-3), which beats external recall's 0.00% in the same cell.

Fixed 15-layer baselines: chess hard up to 42.16%, matching the best recall model (42.22%). Sudoku val <= 4.3%. Prefix sums val 0-81.6% and hard 0%; hard is structurally out of reach with a 60-token receptive field on 512-bit inputs.

Data-reporting error: the sudoku '3e-4' column of Tables 4-5 equals the mean of Table 6's 1e-4 and 3e-4 columns. Examples: GRU internal (24.93 + 28.91)/2 = 26.92; pre external (24.90 + 44.98)/2 = 34.94; GRU internal hard (0.13 + 2.93)/2 = 1.53. The Fig 6 legend (1e-4/3e-4/1e-3) also disagrees with its caption for sudoku.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L1: looping helps narrow Cos-Bochner more than GeGLU on recall
bearing_on_predictions.reason: The paper does not study memorization capacity or FFN type. Its fixed-point account applies only near convergence, and our loops are far from it: GeGLU's relative step is 1.47 at pass 1, and K <= 4 in training. Any K effect on recall is therefore extra weight-tied depth, not attractor dynamics. Its argument that autonomous loops only do 'basin selection' does not limit discrete recall: 32 values, each fact is a basin choice. Its cited prior work (Saunshi et al.) finds that weight-tying trades memorization for reasoning at matched FLOPs, which gives no reason to expect a recall gain. Our GeGLU decline (0.938 / 0.933 / 0.926 at K = 1 / 2 / 4) is about 1 point, single-seed, and comes from models trained separately at each K. It cannot be attributed to expansive dynamics until seeds and SE are added.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L2: looping improves noise robustness (clean-up toward stored states) more for Cos-Bochner
bearing_on_predictions.reason: Supports the mechanism. In the paper's terms, clean-up means the perturbed state lies in an attracting basin, which needs local contraction (rho < 1). Prop 3 case 1 and A.8 say that in that regime perturbations of the starting state are forgotten. Against it: Props 1-2 do not map onto our block the way the brief assumes. In h <- h + a f(LN(h)), g(h) = f(LN(h)) has a Jacobian that is singular everywhere, because LN is invariant to rescaling h and to adding a multiple of the all-ones vector. Combined with the transversality argument the paper uses, this means that for almost all parameters our loop has no fixed points at all in raw state space, not isolated ones. In bios, each pass adds a post-norm vector of fixed RMS, so no fixed point exists unless the norm scale goes to 0. Clean-up can therefore happen only in the normalized/readout state, toward fixed directions of LN(h), with an effective step that shrinks as |h| grows. The paper also gets non-degrading extra iterations only by training with progressive loss over random depths. Training at a fixed K leaves attractors untrained, so K_test > K mostly probes untrained dynamics. And our facts FFN is hetero-associative (key -> value): nothing trains f to send noised keys back toward stored keys.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L3: the narrow kernel has the largest per-pass Jacobian
bearing_on_predictions.reason: Under this framework a large Jacobian at stored states means expansion, so the fixed point is not reachable (rho > 1, case 2). L3 as stated therefore pulls against L2: the narrowest kernel would be the worst at clean-up. What matters for contraction is where the branch eigenvalues lie, not their size. The residual stability condition has the form |1 + lambda| < 1 (Fig 5, Prop 4). A large branch Jacobian with eigenvalues near -1 contracts, while a large one with eigenvalues of positive real part expands. Our probes record rho(J), ||J||_2 and ||J - I||_2, which measure size, not location. Also, by construction the raw-state J has an eigenvalue of about 1 along h, and along the all-ones vector for LayerNorm, so rho(J) >= 1 always. A radius 'below 1 at stored states' therefore cannot occur in our current measure.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L4: looping widens Cos T = 1's seen/held-out gap
bearing_on_predictions.reason: The paper's 'generalization' means extrapolating to harder or longer instances, not wording invariance, and it has no memorization-vs-knowledge experiment. A possible link is speculative. If looping sharpens basins, a held-out-template state outside the stored basin would fail outright instead of partly, which would widen the gap. But that requires contraction near stored states, which the paper never measures in trained nets. Saunshi et al. (cited) would weakly predict the opposite.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L5: Cos T = 2 stays wording-invariant under looping
bearing_on_predictions.reason: There is only conditional mechanistic support. In a contracting regime the end state is locally independent of perturbations of the start (A.8 analogue), so wording variants inside one wide basin would converge, consistent with L5. In an expansive regime, extra passes amplify wording differences, which would break L5. The paper offers no data either way, and with our pre-norm or peri-norm residual loops the question has to be asked of LN(h) and the logits, not raw h.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: Brief's reading that GeGLU's per-pass radius of about 3.3 puts it in the expansive regime, so extra passes drift
bearing_on_predictions.reason: The paper's regimes are defined at a fixed point, and 3.3 was measured at evaluation states on pass 1, where the relative step is 1.47, far from any fixed point. The raw J also includes the eigenvalue-1 directions noted under L3, and |h| grows each pass, which the final LN divides out. The expansion seen by the readout is roughly the tangent-space gain divided by |h_{k+1}|/|h_k|. With a relative step of 1.47 that norm ratio is about 1.8-2.5, so the effective gain is plausibly above 1 but much smaller than 3.3. It has not been measured.

critical_gaps: Props 1-2 do not handle normalization inside the loop. With pre-norm, g(x) = f(x) - x = h(N(x)) has a Jacobian that is singular wherever N is scale-invariant (J_N x = 0). Assumption 1 plus parametric transversality then implies that for almost all theta there are no fixed points, not a countable set. That covers the paper's own 'pre' configuration and ours. The paper never notes this, and its 'basin selection' picture is therefore vacuous in raw state space for pre-norm loops. A.2 asserts that joint fixed points through a normalizing head are dimension zero under an 'analogous' assumption, without checking whether the scale invariance breaks it.

The theory is asymptotic (T -> infinity). At finite T the transient carries continuous input dependence, and Prop 3 even assumes exact convergence at a finite step K, which smooth contracting maps do not do. Treating vanishing input-gradients as 'forgetting the input' is a failure only for algorithmic extrapolation. For associative recall, basin selection is the intended behavior.

The benefit of outer normalization is argued informally. Brouwer gives existence of a fixed point, not reachability or uniqueness. The RMSNorm Jacobian has gain about sqrt(d) gamma / |x| on the tangent space, so it is not contractive in general. Prop 5 holds for any recall model with rho < 1 and never uses outer norm, so the central claim that recall plus outer norm 'reliably' yields the stable regime is not proven.

The three axes are never measured directly on trained networks. There are no convergence residuals, no rho of the actual fixed-point Jacobian, and no measurement of dx*/dx_0. The only spectral measurement is rho(W_x), a recall weight matrix and only one factor of M_ext. It is shown only for non-outer-normalized pre/peri models, and the Fig 7 title says 'spectral norm' while plotting the radius.

rho(W_x) is confounded with learning rate: Fig 6 shows only high LR moves it off its initial value of about 0.6. Failures at rho > 1 could therefore be generic high-LR optimization failures. Fig 7 has about 27 points, only about 6 above 1, with counterexamples: sudoku at rho about 1.1 is non-zero, and prefix sums at rho about 0.87 is zero. The 'normalized accuracy' normalizer is not given, and the sudoku 3e-3 run with 0.00 val (Table 6) does not appear as a zero point in Fig 7.

Training confound for autonomous vs recall (my inference from the stated recipe, not checked in their code). Progressive loss with alpha = 1 runs N ~ U[0, 29] passes without gradients and takes no full-trajectory loss. An autonomous net's input encoder then gets gradient only when N = 0, about 1 batch in 30, while recall nets get input gradients every batch through x_0 injection. The autonomous models' weak hard accuracy may partly come from this, not only from Props 2-3.

Statistics and reporting: 3 seeds, no SE or CIs, comparisons taken as best over an LR grid, and the Fig 3 curves selected by hard accuracy. The '+2 points on chess' advantage of outer norm (42.22% vs 39.29%) is within plausible seed noise. The sudoku column in Tables 4-5 is a mislabeled mix of two LRs, and the Fig 6 legend conflicts with its caption.

The fixed-depth baselines look under-tuned (sudoku val <= 4.3%, prefix-sums val 0-82% for an 11.9M-param model on 32-bit inputs). Their hard prefix-sum task is structurally impossible for them (60-token receptive field vs 512 bits), so 'recall gains are not due to parameters' is weakly supported.
The geometry axis rests only on a 2-D toy that assumes commuting eigenvectors (Table 3). Nothing shows where trained networks sit relative to those regions.

Scope: one looped layer, d = 256, three algorithmic tasks, no recall or memorization task, no FFN-type comparison. The conclusion also contradicts Prop 3 by saying autonomous networks 'succeed on reachability'.
measures_we_lack: A normalized-state (tangent-space) Jacobian. Currently rcdl/facts.py loop_probe and rcdl/bios.py loop_probe take J_k = d(h + a f(LN h))/dh in raw state. That J has an eigenvalue of about 1 along h (and along the all-ones vector for LayerNorm), so rho >= 1 always, and the '< 1 at stored states' test cannot be passed. Report instead the Jacobian of u_k -> u_{k+1} with u = LN(h) (or ln_f(h)): equivalently P_{k+1} J_k P_k scaled by |h_k|/|h_{k+1}|, with P projecting out the h and all-ones directions. Report it at stored (training-fact) states, at noised states, and in bios at seen vs held-out-template states.

The location of the branch spectrum, not just its size: the eigenvalues of B = a J_f J_LN (tangent-projected), and the fraction inside the contraction disk |1 + lambda| < 1 vs outside. This is the residual-form condition from the paper's Fig 5 / Prop 4. ||J - I||_2 alone cannot tell a contracting large Jacobian (eigenvalues near -1) from an expanding one.

Convergence and fixed-point diagnostics out to large K_test (for example 16-64; the paper goes to 500). Per pass, report the absolute update |a f(LN h_k)|, |h_k| growth, |LN(h_{k+1}) - LN(h_k)|, the change in logits, the fraction of predictions that flip between passes (readout-level 'joint fixed point'), and the radial vs tangential share of the update. A falling relative step can come from norm growth alone and is not evidence of approaching a fixed point. In bios, also track the post_ffn_norm scale (1 + w), since each pass adds a fixed-RMS vector.

A trajectory-level clean-up ratio: |LN(h_k^noisy) - LN(h_k^clean)| / |LN(h_0^noisy) - LN(h_0^clean)| per pass. Classify each noisy trajectory's endpoint as the clean trajectory's endpoint (correct basin), another fact's endpoint (wrong basin), or neither (drift). Accuracy under noise alone cannot separate clean-up from drift.

Separate test-time from train-time effects in the noise probe. Currently noise is tested only at the trained K. Also evaluate each K-trained model at K_test = 1 under the same noise draws, and the K = 1 model at K_test > 1. Report robustness relative to clean accuracy, since GeGLU and Cos start at different clean accuracies.

Input-gradient flow through the loop: the norm of dh_K/dh_0, or the gradient norm reaching the attention layers, during training, plus plateau length vs K. Prop 3 case 1 predicts that contraction starves the earlier layers, and those are the name-moving circuits behind the Zucchet plateau.

A depth-randomized training control: train with random K or Bansal-style progressive loss (N no-grad passes plus K grad passes, alpha = 1) so the post-K dynamics are trained. Without it, K_test = 8 > K_train is untrained territory, and degradation there does not show an FFN-intrinsic difference.

Architectural controls from the paper: a recall variant that re-injects the pre-loop state (for example h_{k+1} = h_0 + a f(LN(h_k)), or recall inside the branch) and an outer-norm variant (h_{k+1} = LN_out(h_k + a f(LN h_k))). These test whether Cos's advantage survives once the loop is made stable by design.
Basin counting: cluster the final normalized states at large K_test and compare the number of attractors to the number of values (32) vs facts (8192 x 4).
At least 3 seeds per (FFN, K) cell with SE. The paper's own 3-seed tables have no error bars, and our early GeGLU differences are about 0.5-1.2 points.

reads.title: Hopfield Networks is All You Need (Ramsauer et al., ICLR 2021; arXiv v3, 28 Apr 2021)
reads.sections_read: The full 94-page v3 PDF, converted with pdftotext and read in order: abstract, Sections 1-4 and conclusion; Appendix A.1.1-A.1.9 (energy, CCCP update, global convergence Thms A1-A2, local convergence Lemmas A2-A12 for the global, single-pattern and metastable fixed points, storage Thms A3-A7 with Lemmas A13-A17, one-update retrieval Thm A8, retrieval error Thm A9, learning associations A.1.7, forgetting A.1.8, spurious states A.1.9); A.2 (softmax/lse/Legendre/Lambert lemmas A18-A32); A.3 (binary modern Hopfield nets, Demircigil Thm A10); A.4; A.5 (BERT operating classes, BERT-small training dynamics, Gaussian averaging heads, MIL, UCI, drug design, with Tables 1, 2, A.1-A.5); A.6 (PyTorch layer: multiple updates, variable beta, normalization); and the references. I read the figures (BERT violin and ridge plots, Fig. A.5 Jacobian densities) only through their captions and the extracted median labels; I did not inspect the plots visually. I also read the repo code that the mapping depends on, without editing it: rcdl/facts.py (CosFeatures, loop, loop_probe), rcdl/bios.py (Block.ffn_step with Gemma post-norm, CosFFN, loop_probe), experiments/configs/facts_loops.json and bios_loops.json.
reads.setup: Theory paper with benchmark experiments. Model: a continuous modern Hopfield network with energy E = -lse(beta, X^T xi) + 1/2 xi^T xi + beta^-1 ln N + 1/2 M^2. X = (x_1..x_N) are the stored patterns, M = max ||x_i||, and beta is the inverse temperature. The update xi_new = X softmax(beta X^T xi) is the CCCP step on E. It is auto-associative: the keys are the values, so the state is replaced by a convex combination of the stored patterns. The iteration of this update is what the theory analyses: global convergence of the energy, contraction (Banach) near single patterns, near averages over clusters (metastable states) and near the global mean, storage capacity for random patterns on a sphere of radius M = K sqrt(d-1), and error bounds after one update. The link to transformers: with beta = 1/sqrt(d_k), one update followed by W_V is attention. The A.6 implementation offers multiple updates, but they run in the key space and W_V is applied once after the last update. Experiments: (1) descriptive analysis of attention entropy in pre-trained bert-base-cased, and in a BERT-small model (ELECTRA setting: 12 layers, 4 heads, hidden 256, embedding 128, sequence 128, batch 128) trained for 1.45M steps, about 4 days on one V100; (2) multiple instance learning: DeepRC immune repertoires with about 300k instances per bag, plus Tiger, Fox, Elephant and UCSB (HopfieldPooling, AdamW, 160 epochs, manual hyperparameter search, 5x repeated 10-fold nested CV); (3) 75 small UCI datasets (Hopfield layer after an SNN, SGD lr 0.05, batch 4, 100 epochs, per-dataset grid over beta in {1, 0.1, 0.001}, early stopping); (4) four MoleculeNet drug datasets (HopfieldLayer storing the training set, Adam, 4 epochs, batch 1, grid search). Every experimental layer applies one update; the number of updates and beta are never ablated.
key_results: Convergence (Thms 1-2 / A1-A2): CCCP decreases E monotonically. All limit points are stationary points, which may be saddles. xi_{t+1} - xi_t -> 0. The state xi_t itself converges only if the stationary set at the limiting energy is finite. Bound 0 <= E <= 2M^2 for xi in the simplex of the patterns (Lemma A1).

Jacobian of the update (Eq. 59/78): J = beta X(diag(p) - p p^T)X^T = beta Var_p[x]. It is symmetric and PSD. ||J||_2 <= 2 beta N M^2 m with m = max_i p_i(1-p_i) (Lemma A2), and < 2 beta N M^2 eps if p_max >= 1 - eps. Globally ||J||_2 <= beta m_max^2, where m_max is the largest distance of a pattern from the mean. beta m_max^2 < 1 gives a unique global fixed point near the mean (Lemma A3).

Single-pattern fixed point (Lemmas A5-A7): if Delta_i >= 2/(beta N) + (1/beta) ln(2(N-1) N beta M^2), with separation Delta_i = x_i^T x_i - max_{j!=i} x_i^T x_j, then f maps the ball S_i of radius 1/(beta N M) around x_i into itself and contracts there. So the region where contraction is proven shrinks as 1/(beta N).

One-update retrieval (Thm 4/A8): ||f(xi) - x_i*|| <= ||J^m|| ||xi - x_i*||, with ||J^m|| <= 2 beta N M^2 (N-1) exp(-beta(Delta_i - 2 max{||xi - x_i||, ||x_i* - x_i||} M)). The iteration contracts wherever Delta_i > 2 max{...} M + (1/beta) ln(2(N-1) N beta M^2) (Eq. 183). The prefactor is about 2 beta N^2 M^2, so the bound only drops below 1 when beta Delta is at least about ln(2 N^2 beta M^2).

Retrieval error (Thm 5/A9): ||f(xi) - x_i|| <= 2(N-1) exp(-beta(Delta_i - 2 max{...} M)) M. With ||x_i - x_i*|| and ||x_i - xi|| <= 1/(2 beta M): ||x_i - x_i*|| <= 2e(N-1) M exp(-beta Delta_i). For one update from a query xi, Lemma A4 gives ||x_i - f(xi)|| <= 2 (N-1) exp(-beta c) M, where c is the query's own margin over the other patterns.

Metastable states (Lemmas A8-A12): when l similar patterns carry mass >= 1 - eps, ||J|| <= beta(m_max^2 + 2 eps(2 - eps) M^2). A fixed point near the cluster mean exists in a ball of radius 1/(beta m_max) if beta m_max^2 <= 1 and the cluster centre is separated by Delta_m >= 2M/(beta m_max) - (1/beta) ln((1 - beta m_max^2)/(2 beta (N-l) M max{m_max, 2M})). In the paper's words: 'Iterations that start near the metastable state converge to this metastable state, also if initialized by one of the similar patterns.'

Regimes are set by beta, M, m_max and ||m_x|| (A.6.2): low beta gives global averaging, higher beta gives metastable states and then single patterns. Larger M or a larger associative dimension gives smaller metastable states. The paper states that 'small metastable states ... have largest gradient as shown in Fig. A.5(b)'.

Storage capacity (Thm 3/A5): with probability 1 - p, N >= sqrt(p) c^((d-1)/4) random patterns on a sphere of radius K sqrt(d-1). c >= 3.1546 for beta=1, K=3, d=20, p=0.001; c >= 1.3718 for beta=1, K=1, d=75, p=0.001. Placed patterns: N = 2^(2(d-1)) for beta=1, M=2 sqrt(d-1), d>=4 (Thm A3), and 2^(3(d-1)) for M=5 sqrt(d-1), d>=3 (Thm A4). Expected-separation version: N = 2^((d-1)/4) for beta=1, K=3, d>=17 (Thm A7). These regimes have beta M^2 = K^2(d-1), i.e. very sharp softmaxes.

Binary modern Hopfield nets (Demircigil, Thm A10): N = exp(alpha d)+1 random +-1 patterns. Queries at Hamming radius rho d are recovered in one update with high probability as d -> infinity if alpha < I(1-2 rho)/2. Capacity is traded against the size of the basin of attraction.
Spurious states (A.1.9): the minima of E are the modes of the mixture sum_i exp(beta||x_i||^2/2) G(xi; x_i, beta^-1 I), and such a mixture can have more than N modes. Their number is not bounded.

Hetero-association (A.1.7.2, A.6.2): 'For multiple updates this update rule [xi <- W Y softmax(beta Y^T W^T xi), in the associative space] has to be used'. W_V is applied once after the last update. The gradients with respect to W, W_Q and W_K are all proportional to J (Eqs. 418, 429, 435), so a saturated softmax starves learning.

BERT analysis: k is the smallest number of softmax entries that sum to 0.90. Classes: I (median k > N/2), II (N/8 < k <= N/2), III (N/32 < k <= N/8), IV (k <= N/32). In bert-base-cased, class I dominates the lower layers, classes II and IV the middle layers, class III the last layers. In BERT-small (thresholds divided by 4 for sequence 128), middle-layer heads switch to class IV around step 9,000-10,000, together with the second loss drop, and afterwards 'remain almost unchanged' (small softmax Jacobian).

Benchmarks (one update everywhere). MIL AUC: Tiger 91.3+-0.5, Fox 64.05+-0.4 (below Path encoding 71.2, MInD 70.4, MILES 73.8 and Citation-kNN 63.5... i.e. below the three best baselines), Elephant 94.9+-0.3, UCSB 89.5+-0.8. DeepRC on CMV: AUC 0.832+-0.022 vs SVM-MinMax 0.825+-0.022. UCI, 75 small datasets: average rank difference -3.92 vs SVM -3.23 (p=0.15), SNN -2.85 (p=0.10), RF -2.79 (p=0.05). Drugs: SIDER 0.672+-0.019 and BACE 0.902+-0.023 are best; HIV 0.815 (GCN 0.834) and BBBP 0.910 (RF 0.927) are not.

Derived for our blocks, my algebra not the paper's (1/2). Pre-LN residual block: J_LN(h) h = 0 and J_LN(h) 1 = 0 (scale and shift invariance), so J_block = I + a J_f J_LN has eigenvalue exactly 1 on the centred h and on 1. The per-pass spectral radius is therefore >= 1 for every arm (bios RMSNorm: eigenvalue 1 on h). A Hopfield-like contraction can only show up in the tangent directions. On the normalized sphere, the fixed-point condition is that f(LN h*) is parallel to centred h*, not that f = 0. On inputs of fixed norm M, the unnormalized Gaussian kernel sum equals exp(-beta M^2) Z(u) V softmax(beta X^T u), i.e. Hopfield hetero-retrieval times an input-dependent gain, with beta = 1/sigma^2.

Derived for our blocks (2/2). Assumptions: gamma_LN = 1, random-like state geometry, exact kernel. Facts (d=128, M^2=128): sigma=4 gives beta M^2 = 8; sigma=8 gives beta M^2 = 2. The paper's provable one-update condition at N*A = 32,768 fact states needs beta Delta > ln(2 N^2 beta M^2), about 23.6 (sigma 4) or 22.2 (sigma 8), but beta Delta <= 2 beta M^2 = 16 / 4, so it is unreachable unless training grows the LN gain. The typical self-weight is p_self ~0.07 (sigma 4) and ~2e-4 (sigma 8). At a two-pattern boundary ||J|| = beta Delta/2, about 2.4-4 (sigma 4) or 0.6-1 (sigma 8). Bios (d=256): T=1 gives beta M^2 = 16 and p_self ~0.98-0.99 for 5e4-1e5 stored states; T=2 gives beta M^2 = 8 and p_self ~0.03-0.05. This matches the earlier finding that T=1 memorizes wording and T=2 averages over it. Relative noise 0.1/0.25/0.5 added before the facts block rotates LN(h) by 5.7/14/26.6 degrees and lowers the sigma=4 self-logit by only 0.04/0.24/0.85, against a self-logit of 8.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L1: looping helps narrow Cos-Bochner more than GeGLU on recall
bearing_on_predictions.reason: The theory has three regimes. A kernel that is narrow in the paper's sense (beta Delta >> ln N) is retrieved in one update with error 2(N-1)exp(-beta c)M, so extra passes add almost nothing. A wide kernel converges to its metastable or global average 'also if initialized by one of the similar patterns', so looping at fixed beta cannot turn a mixture into single-fact recall and can pull a correct state into the mixture. Gains from more passes are expected only in the transition band, where ||J^m|| is close to but below 1 and the fixed point is the correct pattern. With gamma_LN = 1, the facts sigma=4 arm is not narrow by the paper's criterion: the required beta Delta of about 23.6 cannot be reached because beta Delta <= 16, and p_self is about 0.07. It may therefore sit in exactly that transition band. If so, a looping gain for sigma 4 over sigma 8 would agree with the paper, but because sigma 4 is intermediate, not because it is narrow. The paper says nothing about GeGLU. It also says nothing about training through the loop at K; it covers only iterating a fixed memory, which corresponds to the K_test sweep of K=1-trained models. Its multi-update guarantees cover auto-associative iteration in key space with W_V applied once. They do not cover a residual block that adds a hetero-associative value on every pass.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L2: looping improves noise robustness (clean-up toward stored states) more for Cos-Bochner
bearing_on_predictions.reason: The theory supports one-update clean-up for a sharp kernel: noise lowers a query's margin c by at most 2||n||M, and the error after one update is exponentially small in beta c. That implies the gain from extra passes is small. Proven contraction holds only in the ball of radius 1/(beta N M), which is negligible at N = 32,768. The paper therefore gives no basin-size guarantee at relative noise 0.1-0.5; Demircigil's result shows that the basin shrinks as capacity grows. Our block also differs from the Hopfield update. The residual never replaces the state, so the noise vector n stays in h. As ||h_k|| grows (relative step 1.47 per pass for GeGLU), LN dilutes n roughly as ||n||/||h_k||. Robustness that improves with K can therefore come from dilution, with no attractor at all. For sigma=4 the lookup weights hardly move at these noise levels (self-logit drop 0.04-0.85 against 8), so dilution is the more likely mechanism in facts. Away from stored states, the unnormalized kernel's gain exp(-beta||u - x_j||^2/2) shrinks the update (a dead zone). In bios, the post-norm instead forces a fixed-RMS step whatever the size of f.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L3: the narrow kernel has the largest per-pass Jacobian
bearing_on_predictions.reason: J = beta Var_p[x]. It is near zero at a saturated stored state (< 2 beta N M^2 eps). It peaks between a few patterns: beta Delta/2 at a two-pattern boundary, about 2.4-4 for sigma 4 and 0.6-1 for sigma 8 with random geometry. It is small again under broad averaging (about beta M^2/d for isotropic patterns, and <= beta m_max^2). A.6.2 likewise says small metastable states have the largest gradient. The paper therefore predicts that the narrow kernel has the largest maximum (at boundaries) but not the largest median at well-stored states. In our residual form, the median radius at stored states should sit at the exact floor of 1, with |J - I| close to 0.
