As worded, L3 is contradicted for the median at stored states and supported for the tail and for boundary states. Bios has a caveat. The probe samples held-out value positions; for T=1 these lie off the stored wording variants, which is between basins. There, post_ffn_norm scales J_f by about 1/||f||, so L3 can come out true at held-out positions for reasons consistent with the paper.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L4: looping widens Cos-Bochner T=1's seen/held-out gap
bearing_on_predictions.reason: The paper gives the mechanism but not the sign. Iteration converges to the fixed point of the basin the query starts in. For T=1, with p_self about 0.98-0.99 at gamma=1 and fixed Omega, each seen wording variant is its own fixed point, so seen accuracy should barely change under looping. Held-out-template states sit between stored variants and get pulled to the nearest one. If that variant is the same fact under another template, the gap closes; if it is the same template under another fact, the gap widens. Which one happens depends on the geometry of the representation, and our test does not measure it. Two caveats weaken the transfer to bios. Omega is trained (cos_train=True), and the RMSNorm gains change beta, so T describes only the initialization. And the Gemma post-norm adds a fixed-RMS update every pass, so a zero-update fixed point cannot exist there.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L5: Cos T=2 stays wording-invariant under looping
bearing_on_predictions.reason: Metastable states are stable fixed points when the within-cluster spread satisfies beta m_max^2 <= 1 and the cluster centre is separated from the other patterns (Lemma A12). Iterations started from any member converge to the cluster average. If T=2's averaging spans the template variants of one fact (p_self about 0.03-0.05, i.e. averaging over 20-40 states), looping should keep or strengthen the invariant fact representation. The support is conditional: if the averaging also spans different facts, iteration drifts toward a larger or global average and recall erodes. The paper offers no test of which case holds. The same caveats apply: beta changes after training, and the post-norm forces a step every pass.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: Early data: GeGLU recall 0.938/0.933/0.926 at K=1/2/4; per-pass spectral radius about 3.3 and relative step 1.47 at K=1
bearing_on_predictions.reason: The paper has nothing on GeGLU. Under its contraction framing, a block whose tangent Jacobian exceeds 1 is in no proven contraction region, so iterating it carries no convergence guarantee, which fits the slight decline with K. Because the radius has an exact floor of 1 in any pre-LN residual block, the 3.3 reflects expansion in tangent directions. A relative step of 1.47 also means f(LN h) is far from parallel to h, so the block is not a fixed-point iteration on the sphere. The 1.2-point decline is about 3 binomial SE at 4,096 evaluation facts (SE about 0.4 points), and seed variance is unknown, so it is not yet a result.

critical_gaps: No experiment iterates the update. Every benchmark layer applies one update. 'Multiple updates' is offered as a feature but never measured, and the claim after Eq. 186 ('This has been confirmed in several experiments') comes with no data. So nothing in the paper shows empirically that iterating helps or what it converges to.

The one-update bound in the title claim has a prefactor of about 2 beta N^2 M^2. It is vacuous until beta Delta_i >= ln(2 N^2 beta M^2), about 21-24 for N ~ 10^4. For patterns on a sphere Delta_i <= 2M^2, which requires beta M^2 >= ~12. The capacity theorems assume M = K sqrt(d-1) with beta = 1, i.e. beta M^2 = K^2 (d-1), far sharper than transformer attention (beta = 1/sqrt(d_k) on LayerNormed keys). That transformer setting is exactly the one the paper equates its update with.

'Stored' is defined by a fixed point inside a ball of radius 1/(beta N M), which shrinks with N and beta. Exponential capacity therefore comes with a vanishing basin of attraction, so the result says nothing about tolerance to noise. Demircigil's binary result makes the capacity-vs-basin trade-off explicit; the continuous theory does not.

Thm A8's estimate of Delta uses E[x^T x - x^T y] = d for a single pair. But Delta_i is a minimum over N-1 others, which is lower by about sqrt(6 d ln N). The argument also mixes Gaussian-component vectors with the M = 2 sqrt(d-1) sphere. So 'Lipschitz constant decreases exponentially with dimension' is overstated for large N.

Global convergence is to stationary points, which may be saddles; the iterates converge only if the stationary set is finite. Spurious fixed points (mixture modes beyond N) are acknowledged but not bounded. The metastable analysis gives sufficient conditions for a fixed point near a cluster mean, but it does not characterize basins, nor which fixed point a given query reaches.

The theory covers the auto-associative update X softmax(beta X^T xi), with keys equal to values and the state replaced. The claimed transformer equivalence concerns one update with a separate W_V, residual connections and LayerNorm, none of which the fixed-point theory covers. The paper's own multi-update mode iterates in key space and applies W_V once.

The BERT 'operating classes' are a one-step entropy statistic (k for 0.90 of the mass) with arbitrary thresholds (N/2, N/8, N/32, divided by 4 for BERT-small). Calling heads 'metastable states' assumes the queries sit near fixed points of an iterated map, which is never checked. The proposed Gaussian averaging heads have no reported results. The training-dynamics claim (class IV heads commit at 9-10k steps, coincide with a loss drop, then freeze) comes from one BERT-small run and is correlational. The text is also internally inconsistent: class IV heads 'remain almost unchanged', yet A.6.2 says small metastable states have the largest gradient.

The benchmarks do not test the theory. Baselines are copied from other papers (whichever source reports the higher AUC). The Hopfield models get per-dataset grid searches. Beta and the number of updates are never ablated. Fox AUC 64.05 is below the three best baselines (70.4-73.8). On UCI the win over SVM, SNN and RF is not significant (p = 0.15/0.10/0.05). Drug design is state of the art on only 2 of 4 datasets. There is no control separating the Hopfield mechanism from plain attention or kNN over stored training data.

Small errors suggest the proofs were not closely checked. Eq. 405 carries an extra factor M. Lemma A25 states the softmax is contractive 'for beta < 2m', whereas its Lipschitz constant 2 beta m requires beta < 1/(2m). The Lemma A10/A11 proofs reuse 'S_i' for S_m.
measures_we_lack: Effective bandwidth after training. The labels T and sigma describe only the initialization: the LN or RMSNorm gain multiplies the effective beta by gamma^2, and bios trains Omega and b. Report beta_eff M^2 per arm at the looped block.

The paper's dimensionless regime numbers, computed at the looped block's LN-space inputs: separations between facts Delta_i, the within-fact spread m_max (over distractors and positions in facts, over templates in bios), then beta_eff Delta vs ln(2 N^2 beta_eff M^2) and beta_eff m_max^2 vs 1. This places each arm in the single-pattern, transition or metastable/global regime before we interpret L1-L5.

Kernel occupancy, the paper's BERT statistic adapted to our layer. Over a bank of stored training states with fact labels, count the states needed to reach 90% of the exact Gaussian-kernel mass at each query, and the fraction of that mass on same-fact states. In bios, split it into same-fact vs same-template.

A fixed-point-on-the-sphere test, per pass: cosine(f(LN h), centred h), and the tangential update ||P_perp f|| / ||h||, where P_perp projects out span{1, h}. The Hopfield correspondence needs the tangential update to vanish at trained states; f = 0 is not required.

A tangent-space Jacobian. The current radius and norm have an exact floor of 1, because J_LN annihilates h and 1 (RMSNorm: h). Report the spectrum of P_perp J_block P_perp, and correct for the 1/||h_k|| shrinkage of J_LN as ||h|| grows across passes.

Jacobians at basin boundaries and at noisy states, not only at clean trained states. Use midpoints between two facts' LN states, and report the maximum and the full distribution. The paper predicts small values at stored states and about beta Delta/2 at two-pattern boundaries.

Clean-up vs dilution: per pass, ||LN(h_k^noisy) - LN(h_k^clean)||, compared with the dilution-only prediction e ||h_0|| / ||h_k||. Measure noise at every K_test in {1, 2, 4, 8} for every trained K, with several noise draws.

An update-only readout: accuracy of head(ln_f(f(LN h))) without h. If f is locally constant, LN(h_0 + K f) tends to LN(f), so this predicts the K_test -> infinity limit. Also extend K_test to 16-32 to find where accuracy settles.

An exact-kernel reference: a normalized softmax or Gaussian lookup over a stored-state bank (or the growing RBF layer) looped in the same way. The random-feature model has D = 16,384 (facts) and 4,096 (bios), fewer than the 32,768+ stored states, with per-pair kernel noise of variance 1/D, so it cannot place one bump per state.

An auto-associative control loop, the paper's multi-update mode: iterate u <- LN(sum_j k(u, x_j) x_j) in state space, then apply the value map once. This is the only setting where the paper's guarantees apply, and it separates retrieval dynamics from hetero-associative drift.

A finer sweep to locate the transition band where the paper expects the largest looping gains: sigma in {2, 3, 4, 6, 8} for facts, T in {0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 4} for bios. Add loop_alpha < 1 (damped steps).

A pure dynamics test: K=1-trained models swept over K_test, kept separate from trained-at-K runs. Add parameter- and compute-matched untied controls (K untied blocks, or a K-times wider FFN) to separate extra compute from tied-weight fixed-point behaviour.
At least 3 seeds per arm, with binomial SEs. Identical bios Cos-Bochner runs differed by 9 points across seeds, and the GeGLU 0.938 -> 0.926 decline is about 3 SE at 4,096 evaluation facts.

For L4 in bios: which stored state is nearest to each held-out-template state (same fact vs same template), plus the pre-post-norm ||f|| at held-out vs seen positions. post_ffn_norm scales the Jacobian by about 1/||f||.
Gradient norms reaching the looped block during training. The paper ties saturated attention to vanishing weight gradients (Eq. 418) and to heads that stop changing.

reads.title: Dense Associative Memory Through the Lens of Random Features (DrDAM), Hoover, Chau, Strobelt, Ram, Krotov, NeurIPS 2024
reads.sections_read: The full arXiv HTML (v1): abstract; sections 1-5 including Algorithm 1, Propositions 1-5, Theorems 1-2 and Corollary 1; Appendix A (limitations), B (error vs number of stored patterns K), C (basis-function ablation), D (TinyImageNet details), E (compute) and F (all proofs: Lemmas 1-3, the proof of Theorem 2, F.2.2). I also opened all six figure images and read values off the log-scale panels of Figs 3, 4A, 5 and 6. I only skimmed the bibliography. To check one point, I simulated the exact model (MrDAM) at the paper's Fig 3/4 settings in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-rcdltesting/67502866-e3ee-5513-b270-94b7a7c21d08/scratchpad/drdam_sim/mrdam.py and mrdam2.py. I also read rcdl/facts.py, rcdl/bios.py (CosFFN, loop) and experiments/configs/{facts,bios}_loops.json to map the paper's quantities onto our runs.
reads.setup:
No training. The paper fixes a Dense Associative Memory energy, E(x) = -(1/beta) log sum_mu exp(-beta/2 ||x - xi_mu||^2) (eq. 11, the L2/RBF kernel; eq. 7 gives a dot-product variant). The exact model, "MrDAM", stores the K patterns. "DrDAM" replaces them with one summed feature vector T = sum_mu phi(sqrt(beta) xi_mu), built from Rahimi-Recht random features. The default is SinCos, phi = [cos(w.x), sin(w.x)]/sqrt(Y) with w ~ N(0, I). Y counts random samples, so T has 2Y entries. Storage is a plain unweighted sum: nothing is fit to data. Iteration is gradient descent on the energy, x <- x - eta grad E. In experiments the gradient comes from JAX autograd of the approximate energy (eq. 10), run with clamping until |dE| < eps; for TinyImageNet, eta = 0.1 for 300-1000 steps. The memory is autoassociative (the values are the patterns themselves), and the grad E = x - softmax(.) Xi form has an explicit decay term.

Experiments:
(D1) Energy and gradient mean absolute error (MAE) of DrDAM vs MrDAM. K = 500 random binary patterns in {0, 1/sqrt(D)}^D, so the typical squared distance between patterns is about 0.5. D = 30, 100, 1000; beta = 10, 30, 40, 50; Y = 40k-500k; 500 queries each at stored patterns, "near" (10% of bits flipped, d^2 = 0.1) and "random" (unstored patterns, d^2 about 0.5).
(D2) Hamming distance between DrDAM and MrDAM fixed points after binarizing at 1/(2 sqrt(D)), same settings with Y = 5k-500k.
Fig 4B: CIFAR-10, K = 10, D = 3072, bottom 50% masked, beta = 40-80, Y = 10k-360k.
App B: K = 50-1000 at fixed Y = 2e5.
App C: Cos, SinCos, Exp and ExpExp features on the Letter dataset (D = 16, K = 500, beta = 1-60, Y = 40k-800k).
Theory: a trajectory-divergence bound (Thm 2 / Cor 1). Hardware: one L40S GPU, JAX.
key_results: Fig 3 energy MAE at stored patterns (K=500 binary, SinCos): about 1e-3 at Y=40k down to 3-4e-4 at Y=500k, almost the same for every beta in {10,30,40,50} and every D in {30,100,1000} (my plot reading).

Fig 3 energy MAE near stored patterns (10% bit flips), my plot reading. D=100: beta=50 3.2e-2 (Y=40k) to 4.3e-3 (500k); beta=30 4e-3 to 1.05e-3; beta=10 8.5e-4 to 2.5e-4. D=30 and D=1000 are similar. That makes beta=50 about 4-9x beta=30 and 14-38x beta=10. The text claims about 10x and 100x 'across all Y', which overstates what the plot shows.

Fig 3 random (far) queries, D>=100, beta=50: energy MAE about 7-9e-2, flat from Y=40k to 500k, near the random-guess line (about 1.3e-1). Gradient MAE at D=100/1000, beta in {40,50}, is at or above the random-guess level (about 5.5) for every Y up to 500k. Exception: D=100, beta=40 energy improves from 8e-2 to 1.2e-2. The text says the far/high-D beta=50 error 'approaches 1000x' beta=10; my reading gives about 100-400x.

Fig 3 gradient MAE at stored patterns grows with D while energy MAE does not. At Y=500k, beta>=30: about 1.6e-2 (D=30), 3.2e-2 (D=100), 7.5e-2 (D=1000), roughly proportional to sqrt(D) (my reading). So the paper's statement that errors 'remain the same across D' holds for energies only.

Fig 4A retrieval Hamming error, DrDAM vs MrDAM fixed points (0.5 = random). Near, D=100, beta=50: 0.14 at Y=5k, about 0 for Y>=160k. Near, D=100, beta=40: 0.45 to 0.15. Near, D=1000, beta=50: about 0.16 for Y<=200k, 0.08 at 400k, about 0.01 at 500k, a threshold rather than a gradual decline. Random queries, D=100/1000, beta=40/50: 0.48-0.5 at every Y except D=100, beta=40 (0.48 to 0.12). The authors note that at or near stored patterns, high beta retrieves better than low beta.

Fig 4B (CIFAR-10, K=10, D=3072, half the image clamped): DrDAM gives noise at small Y, then switches to meaningful completions past a threshold Y that grows with beta. Meaningful from about 40k at beta=40, and only at 360k at beta=80. So more features do help at high beta; the number needed rises steeply.

App B / Fig 5 (Y=2e5 fixed). Near stored patterns, beta=50: energy MAE rises from about 1.5e-2 at K=50 to about 0.5 (D=30) and about 1 (D=100, 1000) at K=1000. At stored patterns: about 2e-3 to 3e-2. Near-pattern gradient error at D=1000, beta=50 reaches random-guess level (about 7) by K=1000. The largest K/Y tested is 0.005.

App C / Fig 6 (Letter, D=16, K=500): trigonometric features beat positive random features (Exp, ExpExp) by about 10-100x on gradient MAE at beta>=10, for example about 1e-4 to 1e-3 vs about 5e-2 to 9e-2 at beta=30-60. SinCos is about 1.3-1.5x better than Cos with random phase, our layer's form (beta=60 gradient: 6e-4 vs 9e-4 at Y=40k; 1.6e-4 vs 2.1e-4 at 800k). But SinCos with Y samples has 2Y dimensions, so this comparison is not dimension-matched.

Thm 2: ||x_L - x_hat_L|| <= 2 eta L C1 K e^{beta E(x)} sqrt(D/Y) [1 - (eta L B)^L] / (1 - eta L B), with Lipschitz constant B = 1 + 2 K beta e^{beta/2} (Lemma 2). Cor 1, with eta = C2/(L B): bound = C1 C2 e^{beta(E(x) - 1/2)} sqrt(D/Y) / (beta(1 - C2)).

Fig 1/2 (TinyImageNet, beta=60, Y=1.8e5 or 2e5, eta=0.1, 300-1000 steps): DrDAM reaches visually the same fixed points as MrDAM, though the Fig 2 completions are visibly speckled. In Fig 1B, one DrDAM energy trace sits on a plateau near 0.01 long after MrDAM has converged, so the approximation can slow relaxation.

My exact-MrDAM simulation (eq. 11, K=500, the paper's binary patterns, eta=0.1, to convergence). For D=30 with beta<=40, and D=100 and D=1000 with beta<=30, every query (at, near or far) converges to one centroid state: the maximum softmax weight is 0.002 = 1/K, and no memory is retrieved. Stored patterns are retrieved (Hamming 0, max weight 0.94-0.998) only at beta>=40 (D=100, 1000) or beta=50 (D=30). Far queries go to the centroid at every beta for D=100 and 1000. This matches Fig 4A, where the beta=30, D=1000 trace is identical in the at, near and random columns (about 0.49 at 5k, about 0.1 at 500k).

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L1: looping helps narrow Cos-Bochner more than GeGLU on recall
bearing_on_predictions.reason: The task's rationale (narrow-kernel random-feature error compounds, so K_test = 8 should degrade) is only partly supported. Near stored states, iteration at high beta corrects errors instead of compounding them: at Fig 4A near, D=100, beta=50, the fixed-point error is 0 for Y>=160k, and high beta retrieves better than low beta. The compounding bound (Thm 2) is vacuous at the tested settings. Divergence happens only for far queries. Three structural gaps limit transfer to our L1. (i) Our W_o (and W, b in bios) is trained by least squares, not a summed T = sum phi(xi), so the paper's K/Y error scaling does not apply. (ii) Our memory is heteroassociative, runs 1-8 passes with a = 1 and has no decay term, while the paper runs autoassociative energy descent for hundreds of steps at eta = 0.1. (iii) App A says outright that it does not study different numbers of steps, so it says nothing about testing at K_test = 8 a model trained at K. One relevant point: Fig 1B shows random-feature dynamics can relax more slowly, which would reduce the benefit of a small K.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L2: looping improves noise robustness (clean-up toward stored states) more for Cos-Bochner
bearing_on_predictions.reason: For an autoassociative narrow-kernel memory the paper does show clean-up: 10%-bit-flip queries reach the exact fixed points at beta=50 with enough features (Fig 4A). The task argues that noise 0.5 is the paper's badly approximated 'far' regime. My rough kernel-unit mapping says otherwise. It assumes ||LN h||^2 about 128 and isotropic noise, and ignores competitor states closer than random. Relative noise e gives d^2/(2 sigma^2) of about 4e^2 at sigma=4, so e=0.5 gives an exponent near 1 (k about 0.37). The paper's 'near' condition at the matching beta (about 32) has exponent about 1.6, and its 'random' condition about 8. So all three of our noise levels are near queries in the paper's sense, and the far-query failure is not evidence against L2. The paper's clean-up mechanism, though, needs values equal to stored states plus a contraction term. Our FFN writes attribute-value directions into h without a -h term, so any robustness gain from looping would come from repeatedly adding the same value, not from attractor clean-up. The paper cannot tell us which of these we will see.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L3: the narrow kernel has the largest per-pass Jacobian
bearing_on_predictions.reason: For: Lemma 2's Lipschitz bound 1 + 2K beta e^{beta/2} grows quickly with beta. Also, gradient (derivative-feature) error grows about as sqrt(D) at stored patterns while energy error does not (Fig 3). That fits random-feature derivative noise scaling with ||omega|| ~ sqrt(d)/sigma, which would inflate a narrow kernel's measured Jacobian with feature noise. Against: a Lipschitz upper bound is not the local Jacobian. At a stored state with a saturated kernel the exact update's local Jacobian is near zero (strong contraction); at basin boundaries it is large. A narrow kernel could therefore show the smallest Jacobian at clean evaluation states and the largest between states. The paper never measures local Jacobians.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L4: looping widens Cos T=1's seen/held-out gap
bearing_on_predictions.reason: Weak, indirect support. The approximation holds near stored states and fails for queries at typical inter-pattern distance, with no improvement up to Y=5e5 at beta>=40, D>=100. The threshold Y needed rises steeply with beta (Fig 4B). By my estimate (RMS-normed d=256 states with ||x||^2 about 256, kernel exp(-||x-y||^2/(32T))), bios T=1 corresponds to paper-beta about 64 for unrelated states, above the paper's worst beta=50, and uses only 4k features. The Cos feature noise floor of about 1/sqrt(2*4096) = 0.011 then resolves only pairs closer than about 0.53x the random-pair distance. Seen templates may count as near and held-out ones as far, so extra passes would help seen and not held-out. The transfer is weak: Omega and b are trained in bios, so the features no longer estimate a Gaussian kernel, and post_ffn_norm adds a fixed-RMS vector every pass, so no fixed point exists.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L5: Cos T=2 stays wording-invariant under looping
bearing_on_predictions.reason: For: lower beta keeps energies, gradients and fixed points accurate for all query types (beta=10 errors stay about 10-100x lower at every Y, D and query position). Against: my exact simulation shows that at the paper's K=500 load, iterating a wide kernel (beta<=30) collapses every query to one centroid attractor. T=2 maps to paper-beta about 32 under my rough mapping. For an iterated autoassociative smoother, a wide kernel risks blending facts rather than stabilizing them. Whether this matters for our heteroassociative, post-normed loop is untested.

critical_gaps: Retrieval error is measured against MrDAM's fixed point, never against the stored pattern, and the paper never checks whether MrDAM itself retrieves memories. My simulation shows that at beta<=30 (all D) and beta=40 (D=30), MrDAM sends every query to a single centroid. At low beta the at, near and random columns of Fig 4A are therefore the same experiment (identical traces at beta=30, D=1000), and 'low beta is accurate' partly means 'approximates trivial one-attractor dynamics'. Memories are actually retrieved only at beta>=40-50, which is where DrDAM is worst.

Binarizing at exactly 1/(2 sqrt(D)) puts the centroid state, where far queries end, almost on the threshold: per-entry margin is about 0.022/sqrt(D) for K=500. A small L2 deviation then flips about half the bits, so the '0.5 = retrieving random noise' result for far queries may reflect a small L2 error around a centroid target rather than a random retrieval. L2 distances are never reported.

The D effect is confounded with distance concentration. Patterns are normalized so d^2 is about 0.5 +/- 0.5/sqrt(D); at D=30 some stored patterns lie much closer to a random query than at D=1000, so the kernel signal of the nearest pattern differs by D. Pointwise random-feature kernel error does not depend on D; the gradient error's D dependence probably comes from autograd through features with ||omega|| ~ sqrt(beta D). Neither is separated out.

Theory and experiments use different estimators. Lemma 3 / Thm 2 bound the ratio estimator of eq. 32, which needs R = sum phi(xi) xi^T (Y x D storage) and nonnegative kernel estimates; trigonometric features violate that, and the authors clip. The experiments use autograd of the approximate energy (eq. 10). Assumption A2 has a sign error (exp(+...)) and drops the beta dependence of the random-feature error; eq. 54's second term is zero as written; Lemma 2 uses ||Xi|| <= K where sqrt(K) suffices.

The bound is vacuous where tested. B = 1 + 2K beta e^{beta/2} is about 3.6e15 at K=500, beta=50, so Cor 1's step size is about 1e-16/L, while experiments use eta = 0.1 for hundreds of steps. The 'tight fit' of bound curves in Fig 3 must use unreported, fitted C1 and C2, so it tests only the 1/sqrt(Y) shape. The bound is also overlaid on single-step gradient errors, not on trajectory divergence.

'Adding features does not help at high beta and D' holds only within Y <= 5e5. Fig 4A (D=1000, beta=50, near) and Fig 4B show sharp thresholds above which retrieval recovers, so the right reading is that the required Y grows steeply (roughly as e^{beta d^2} under a signal-to-noise view), not that features never help.

The headline ratios are overstated relative to the plots: about 4-9x and 14-38x by my reading vs the claimed 10x and 100x near stored patterns; about 100-400x vs the claimed 'approaches 1000x' far away.

No variance over random-feature draws. Error bars are SEM over queries only, and Fig 4A has none. Fig 4A traces are visibly non-monotone in Y (D=30, beta=40 at stored patterns: 0.27, 0.10, 0.03, 0.03, 0.10, 0, 0.07, 0.12, 0.07), and D=30 values sit near multiples of 1/30, which suggests few queries per point (my inference). Step size and convergence epsilon for Fig 4A are not stated.

In Fig 6 the 'at stored patterns' and 'at new data' gradient panels show identical values at every point for every beta, which looks like a plotting duplication. The Cos vs SinCos comparison is not dimension-matched (SinCos has 2Y dims), and the ablation uses one 16-dimensional dataset.

The ~20% parameter-reduction claim (Fig 2: 20 x 12288 = 245,760 vs Y = 2e5) conflicts with SinCos producing a 2Y = 4e5-dimensional T (sec. 4.1 indexes alpha in [[2Y]]). It also ignores the D x Y random projection, which is regenerated from a seed at O(DY) compute per step.

Coverage is thin, as App A admits: random binary patterns plus a few images, no learned or structured data, and no study of step size or number of iterations differing from MrDAM. Storage is a plain sum with no learning, so nothing tests random features with a trained readout, which is our case.
measures_we_lack: An exact-kernel reference, the analog of MrDAM: evaluate the looped facts model with the trained W_o but a fresh random-feature draw, or at larger width (4k / 16k / 64k at fixed sigma). This separates gains from the kernel itself from gains from one particular feature draw, and detects the paper's threshold behavior. Also give the variance across random-feature seeds, not only training seeds.

State quantities in kernel units for each arm. Report the beta-equivalent (typical d^2/(2 sigma^2) between evaluation states: my rough estimate is about 8 at facts sigma=4, about 2 at sigma=8, about 16 at bios T=1 and about 8 at T=2). Report the distance to the nearest competing stored state, and the share of kernel values above the feature noise floor of about 1/sqrt(2w) (about 0.0055 at w=16,384; about 0.011 at w=4,096).

Noise graded out to genuinely far queries: relative noise about 1-1.5, i.e. the typical inter-state distance. The current 0.1/0.25/0.5 are all 'near' in kernel units at sigma=4. Use several noise draws per level (currently one fixed draw per e), and report noise in kernel units.

Fixed-point and trajectory diagnostics per pass: ||h_{k+1} - h_k||, the distance from the noisy-start state to the clean-start state after each pass (the paper's fixed-point comparison), the logit margin, and K_test out to 16-32. Accuracy alone, like the paper's binarized Hamming error, can hide or exaggerate small state deviations.

A step-size and decay control: a in {0.1, 0.5, 1}, and a contractive variant h <- (1 - a) h + a f(LN(h)). The paper's attractor results rely on eta = 0.1, a decay term and hundreds of steps; ours has a = 1, no decay, and at most 8 passes.

Jacobians at three kinds of points: clean evaluation states, noisy states, and states interpolated between two stored states. The paper's evidence is a global Lipschitz bound, which can disagree in sign with local Jacobians at stored states.

A load sweep: vary N at fixed width, to see whether any looping benefit depends on items per feature. Paper error rises sharply with K at fixed Y (App B); our facts load is about 32k facts on 16k features, far beyond the paper's maximum K/Y of 0.005.

An autoassociative control: a Cos-Bochner block trained to map noisy states to clean states. This tests whether DAM-style clean-up appears at all, as distinct from repeated value addition in our heteroassociative FFN.

For bios, a fixed-feature arm (Omega and b frozen) next to the trained-feature arms, so the random-feature kernel picture applies; and a run without post_ffn_norm in the looped passes, so a fixed point can exist.
A SinCos-feature variant at matched dimension, to check whether the paper's lower error for SinCos changes the narrow-kernel looping result.

reads.title: Kernel Memory Networks: A Unifying Framework for Memory Modeling (Iatropoulos, Brea, Gerstner; NeurIPS 2022, arXiv v3 23 Jul 2024)
reads.sections_read: Full v3 PDF, 24 pages, extracted locally with pdftotext: Abstract; Sections 1 (Introduction, contributions, related work), 2 (Background), 3.1-3.4 (binary hetero- and auto-associative SVM networks, SDM, modern Hopfield, capacity, iterative learning, generalization, pseudoinverse rule), 4.1-4.2 (continuous patterns, Property 4, the Exp-beta network, Properties 5-7, comparison with softmax), 5 (Discussion), references; Appendices A.1-A.2, B.1-B.2, C, D, E.1-E.4.2 (proofs of Properties 4-9.2), F. I looked at Figures C.1 and E.1 as rendered images. Figures 1, 2 and B.1 I read only through their captions and text.
reads.setup: This is a theory paper. It trains no network on real data and has no transformers. Each output neuron is treated as an independent kernel machine. For binary patterns it is a max-margin SVM (Eq. 3), giving s_out = sgn((A ⊙ X_out) K(X_in, s_in) - θ). For continuous patterns it is a minimum-norm kernel interpolator. A hetero-associative memory is one feed-forward step. It becomes recurrent (auto-associative) only when X_out = X_in, and is then iterated synchronously with the same weights: s <- sgn(...) or s <- X K^+ K(X, s). The update replaces the state; there is no residual form s <- s + f(s) and no normalization layer. Weights come in closed form (Lagrange multipliers, K^-1) and are not trained by gradient. The one exception is Appendix C: a stochastic batch perceptron on one binary neuron, N = 100, pair features, lr 1e-5, 20M iterations, 20 runs. The SDM is shown to be a random-feature hetero-associative network with a one-shot readout (A = 1), the same family as our fixed-W Cos-Bochner layer. Continuous memory uses the exponential-power kernel exp(-(|x - y|/r)^β); the Gaussian kernel is β = 2. That kernel is analysed only in the limit β -> ∞. The simulations are: Fig. E.1, the pattern count at which some pairwise distance falls below 2r (N = 10-70, 1000 runs, σ = 0.45-0.6); Fig. 2, 17 patterns on S^2; Fig. B.1, SDM kernel curves at N_in = 50.
key_results: Property 1 (binary, hetero-associative): solving the SVM per output neuron gives s_out = sgn((A ⊙ X_out) K(X_in, s_in) - θ). Kanerva's SDM is the special case A = 1, θ = 0, ϕ = Θ(Zx - b), i.e. random features with a one-shot readout, which the paper calls suboptimal. SDM capacity O(N_ϕ) with a constant of about 0.1 is stated by citing [12, 31], not derived.

Properties 2.1/2.2: setting X_out = X_in turns the network into a recurrent auto-associative one. The modern Hopfield network is the case A = 1, θ = 0, k = F'. The classical Hopfield network is the linear-kernel case.

Capacity heuristic M_max ≈ 2 D_VC (binary ±1 inputs, general position): about 2N for a linear kernel, O(N^p) for a degree-p polynomial, O(e^N) for the exponential kernel. One-shot Hebbian storage, the support-vector-proliferation regime from Ardeshir et al. (N ≳ 2M log M), gives M_max ~ N/(2 log N) (App. A.2).

App. C (single binary neuron, N = 100, pair features, 20 runs): iterative SBP training stays close to Gardner's optimal margin and reaches zero margin at about 0.7 N^2 patterns. The one-shot modern-Hopfield rule reaches zero margin at about 0.05 N^2. Same kernel, more than 10x apart, purely from the learning rule.

Property 4 (continuous patterns, synchronous update s <- X K^+ K(X, s), K^+ = K^-1 when ϕ(X) has full column rank): every stored pattern is a fixed point. If the patterns are attracting, the minimum-norm interpolation maximizes a lower bound on basin size, via ||J||_2 <= ||J||_F <= ||W||_F ||J_ϕ||_F and the set {||J|| < 1} (App. E.1). That the patterns are attracting is assumed, not shown.

Exp-beta kernel exp(-(|x - y|/r)^β): r roughly sets the radius of attraction and β the steepness of the basin wall. A Gaussian kernel is β = 2 at any width. Property 5.1 (β -> ∞, minimum pairwise distance > r): K -> I and the update becomes s <- X Θ(r - ||X - s||), a hard ball lookup in which K^-1 plays no role.

Properties 5.2/5.3 (β -> ∞, minimum pairwise distance > 2r): a state within r of a pattern converges to it in one step. A state farther than r from every pattern reaches an 'agnostic' state by step 2: the origin, or the pattern closest to the origin. There are no spurious attractors.

Property 6 (β -> ∞, patterns ~ N(0, I_N), large N, separation > 2r): recovery succeeds in at least 50% of trials up to noise variance σ²_max = r²/N, i.e. relative noise of about r/sqrt(N). For bit flips (Property 9.1): ρ_max = r²/4N.

Property 7 (β -> ∞, N >> 1, σ²_max ≲ 1/2, pairwise distances treated as independent): M_max >= 2 sqrt(sqrt(πN)(1 - 2σ²_max)) exp(N(1 - 2σ²_max)²/8). Property 8 (patterns on S^(N-1)): M_max >= sqrt(sqrt(8πN)(1 - 2r²)) exp(N(1 - 2r²)²/4). In Fig. E.1 (N = 10-70, 1000 runs, which test only the geometric criterion) the bound is loose by up to about 8x: at σ = 0.45, N = 70, roughly 800 simulated versus roughly 100 from the bound. It is tighter at σ = 0.6.

Sec. 4.2: the softmax (Ramsauer) network at zero temperature is an argmax, whose basins are Voronoi cells, the largest possible; it always converges to some pattern. Exp-beta basins are balls, smaller, and can return the agnostic state. Fig. 2: 17 patterns on S^2, with ball radius set to half the minimum pairwise distance.

My own calculation, not in the paper. It applies Property 8 (β -> ∞, random states) to our sizes and assumes LayerNorm gain 1. For 32,768 random states on S^127, balls stop overlapping only below a chord radius of 0.49 of the state norm, which is about relative noise 0.53. Facts σ = 4: r = sqrt(2)σ = 5.66, which is 0.50 of the LN norm sqrt(128); that is relative noise e ≈ 0.55. Facts σ = 8: r = 1.0 of the norm (e ≈ 1.73), larger than the random inter-state chord sqrt(2), so the basins overlap. Bios (d = 256, RMSNorm, kernel exp(-|Δ|²/(2T·16))): T = 1 gives r = 0.354 of the norm (e ≈ 0.37); T = 2 gives r = 0.50 (e ≈ 0.55). Gaussian weight of a state's own stored point at the tested noise e = 0.1 / 0.25 / 0.5: 0.96 / 0.79 / 0.43 for σ = 4 and 0.99 / 0.94 / 0.81 for σ = 8. Kernel value between two random states: 3.4e-4 for σ = 4, 0.135 for σ = 8.

Clean stored inputs are already fixed points, and at β -> ∞ any state within the radius converges in one step, so extra passes add nothing to clean recall. Our facts FFN is hetero-associative (name state to value), so the theory gives it no fixed points to iterate toward. The readout is an argmax over 32 values; the paper's softmax comparison says argmax already gives Voronoi basins, the largest possible, so a narrow-kernel clean-up pass cannot enlarge the final decision regions. The paper therefore gives no reason for looping to favour narrow Cos. If L1 shows a gain, the paper's own capacity view suggests a different cause. The σ = 4 layer stores 32,768 random-label facts on 16,384 fixed features, a load of 2, which is the zero-margin limit under M_max ≈ 2 D_VC; composing passes adds effective features, i.e. capacity, not dynamics. A wide kernel's matrix is ill-conditioned (random-pair kernel 0.135 vs 3.4e-4), which forces larger readout weights and pushes its Jacobian up. bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L4: looping widens Cos T = 1's seen/held-out gap
bearing_on_predictions.reason: The support is weak and concerns mechanism only. A narrow r means small basins. A held-out template whose states sit farther than r from every seen-template state gets the agnostic, near-zero kernel output, and Property 5.3 says later passes cannot pull it in, while seen states receive the trained write on every pass. That would widen the gap. The paper's r trade-off (high capacity, low tolerance) and its reading of Krotov and Hopfield's results (too-flexible kernels overfit) both fit T = 1 memorizing wording. T = 1's radius is about 0.354 of the RMS-normed state norm (e ≈ 0.37). Caveats: in bios, post_ffn_norm rescales any FFN output, including a near-zero agnostic one, to fixed RMS, so a far-from-stored state gets a full-size write in an arbitrary direction on every pass. The paper's 'agnostic = 0' does not hold there, though this could widen the gap through added noise. Ω is also trained, so the effective kernel is not T's Gaussian. The paper presents no held-out-generalization data of its own.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L5: Cos T = 2 stays wording-invariant under looping
bearing_on_predictions.reason: The support is weak. A larger r gives larger basins that can contain held-out wording variants. In the β -> ∞ theory iteration does not change basin geometry (states inside a basin converge in one step), so the invariance T = 2 shows at K = 1 should persist at K > 1 if the layer acts as a kernel memory. A larger r costs capacity (Properties 7/8). For 32,768 random states in d = 256, Property 8 gives a non-overlap limit of r ≈ 0.56 of the norm; T = 2 has r ≈ 0.50. Basins should therefore not yet overlap, unless the number of stored bios states is much larger or the states are clustered. Post-norm rescaling and trained Ω weaken the mapping from theory to model. The paper says nothing about how training at K > 1 changes the learned kernel.

critical_gaps: All the quantitative continuous-memory results (Properties 5.1-9.2: one-step convergence, the agnostic state, σ²_max = r²/N, exponential capacity) hold only at β -> ∞. There the kernel is an indicator, K = I and K^+ plays no role, so the results describe a hard ball lookup, not a Gaussian (β = 2) kernel memory such as Cos-Bochner. Finite β is covered by one remark ('increasingly fuzzy') with no analysis or simulation.

No recall dynamics are simulated for any continuous network. Fig. E.1 counts patterns until some pairwise distance falls below 2r, which is the geometric premise, not recall under noise. Property 6 is never checked by simulation. The only learning experiment (App. C) is a single binary neuron.

'Maximal noise robustness' is defined as the margin in feature space (Eq. 2-3), but the text describes it as the input-space distance to the decision boundary. These coincide only for a linear ϕ. For translation-invariant kernels, input-space robustness also depends on ϕ's Lipschitz constant (∝ 1/σ), so narrow and wide kernels are not compared on equal terms.

Property 4 assumes the patterns are attracting. The 'basin subset' {s : ||J_s|| < 1} is not shown to be mapped into itself, which the Banach argument needs. The Frobenius / Cauchy-Schwarz chain is loose, so minimum-norm weights minimize an upper bound on the Jacobian, not the basin. The ill-conditioning of K for wide kernels, which inflates K^-1 and W, is not discussed.

Kernel capacity scalings (O(N^p), O(e^N)) are VC-dimension heuristics for binary inputs (M ≈ 2 D_VC, assuming features in general position). Agreement with earlier proofs (SDM about 0.1 N_ϕ, Hopfield N/(2 log N)) is asserted, not shown.
Property 7 treats pairwise distances as independent. Its lower bound is loose by up to about 8x in Fig. E.1 (σ = 0.45), and simulations stop at N = 70.
Maximizing each neuron's margin is not the same as maximizing basins for the coupled recurrent dynamics. In the binary case this step rests on citations [18, 32].

Only synchronous replacement updates s <- F(s) are covered. Residual updates (s <- s + f(s)), normalization layers, gradient-trained deep networks and transformers are absent; the link to the implicit max-margin bias of gradient descent is a citation only. Most important for us: the paper says nothing about iterating a hetero-associative map (X_out != X_in), which has no stored fixed points.
The connection to attention is qualitative.
measures_we_lack: Fixed-point check over all test passes. rel_step_median (|a f(LN(h))|/|h| at clean states) already measures this, but only over the trained K passes. Extend it to every pass up to K_test = 8 to see whether the trajectory settles (f -> 0) or keeps drifting. For GeGLU at K = 1 it is already 1.47, so its clean states are not fixed points.

Jacobian on the tangent space. With pre-LN (facts) or pre-RMSNorm (bios), J h = h exactly, and in facts LayerNorm also gives J 1 = 1. So the spectral radius and spectral norm are >= 1 for every model, and the paper's attraction criterion ||J||_2 < 1 can never be met. Report the norm of P J P with P projecting out h (and 1). Report the norm of the product J_K...J_1 along the trajectory (the finite-time noise gain), not medians of per-pass values.

Only accuracy above this baseline counts as clean-up. Without it, the growth of |Σ f| with K, against a noise norm fixed at e|h0|, can mimic clean-up.

The paper predicts the same curve shape for both, because both have β = 2.

Jacobian as a function of noise level e. The narrow kernel should be flat (J ≈ I) at clean states, with a wall near |Δ| ≈ σ, i.e. e ≈ 0.37 for σ = 4 and e ≈ 0.88 for σ = 8.

Capacity and compute controls for L1. Cos width x2 and x4 at K = 1: the current load is 32,768 facts on 16,384 features, i.e. 2, at the Cover/Gardner limit. Add an untied K-pass control and a GeGLU matched on trained parameters (Cos W_o has about 2.1M trained parameters, GeGLU width 512 about 0.2M).
A noise / clean-up test in bios. None exists; add one at value-predicting positions, split by seen and held-out templates.

Positive control showing the architecture can clean up at all: a looped Cos block given an auto-associative target. Options: train with noise injected before the loop, or penalize f(LN(h*)) for passes after the first so that clean states become fixed points.
Noise at K_test != K_train, e.g. models trained at K = 1 run for 2-8 passes under noise, to separate learned trajectories from intrinsic clean-up.
