reads.title: A review of mean-shift algorithms for clustering (Carreira-Perpinan, arXiv 1503.00687, March 2015; chapter for the CRC Handbook of Cluster Analysis)
reads.sections_read: I read the full arXiv v1 PDF (28 pages), extracted with pdftotext, line by line. That covers the abstract, Sec. 1 introduction, and all of Sec. 2: 2.1 MS vs BMS, bandwidth, kernel, scale-space, matrix form, out-of-sample mapping, pros and cons; 2.2 origins; 2.3 theory (mode geometry, MS convergence, eq. 5 Jacobian, path properties, basins, BMS convergence, the Gaussian-data BMS analysis, generalized BMS); 2.4 relations to spectral clustering, bilateral filtering and other algorithms; 2.5 extensions (tracking, manifold and graph data, medoidshift, score-matching MS, rankings, functional data); 2.6 manifold denoising with MBMS; 2.7 acceleration. Also read: Sec. 3 on K-modes and Laplacian K-modes, with Table 1; Sec. 4 on applications (Figs. 5-8); Sec. 5 conclusion and open problems; Appendix A on connected components (Fig. 9); and the reference list. Figure graphics could not be seen as images, so only their captions and in-text descriptions were read. To check how the paper maps onto our measures, I also read the repo code: /home/user/rcdltesting/rcdl/facts.py (CosFeatures, FactsModel.loop, loop_probe at lines 177-206), /home/user/rcdltesting/rcdl/bios.py (CosFFN, loop_probe at lines 657-703), and experiments/configs/facts_loops.json and bios_loops.json.
reads.setup: This is a review chapter. It contains no new experiments, and it states its theory "without proof", citing mostly the author's own papers ([9],[10],[13],[14],[15]). The object of study is a Gaussian kernel density estimate (KDE) p(x) = (1/N) sum_n K(||(x - x_n)/sigma||^2) over N data points in R^D. It uses one isotropic bandwidth sigma, equal weights 1/N, and mostly the Gaussian kernel. Mean-shift (MS) iterates x <- f(x) = sum_n p(n|x) x_n. The weights p(n|x) are normalized softmax posteriors (they sum to 1), and the averaged values are the data points themselves, in the same space as the iterate. MS runs from every data point with the data held fixed, and each mode defines one cluster. Blurring mean-shift (BMS) moves the dataset itself: X <- X P(X), with P the random-walk (stochastic) matrix, which gives a nonlinear iterated filter. After either algorithm, a connected-components step with threshold epsilon merges numerically distinct endpoints. The review also covers: generalized BMS, X <- X phi(P), with an over-relaxed step (1 - eta) I + eta P; manifold-blurring MS (MBMS, which removes the tangential component of the step); K-modes and Laplacian K-modes; and acceleration methods. Illustrations are single examples: a 2D toy (Fig. 1); the 50x50 cameraman image as N = 2,500 points in 3D (i, j, intensity) (Figs. 5 and 6); a 1,000-point noisy spiral with 100 outliers (Fig. 3); MNIST at D = 784 (Figs. 4 and 7); and robot-arm and tongue-shape inverse problems (Fig. 8). Nothing is trained in the deep-learning sense. The only thing iterated is the fixed-point map x <- m(x), or X <- X P(X).
key_results: Gaussian MS is an EM algorithm, and MS with non-Gaussian kernels is a generalized EM algorithm (citing [10],[14]). Each Gaussian MS iterate increases the density or leaves it unchanged, and convergence takes infinitely many iterations. With the Epanechnikov kernel MS converges in a finite number of steps, since one MS step equals one Newton step on a piecewise-quadratic KDE. Not every valid kernel gives a convergent MS (counterexample cited from [29]). For kernels that do converge, the limit is a mode for most starting points but can be a saddle or minimum.

Eq. 5 (Gaussian kernel, isotropic sigma, linearized AT a mode x*): J(x*) = Sigma(x*)/sigma^2, where Sigma(x*) = sum_n p(n|x*)(x_n - x*)(x_n - x*)^T is the local posterior covariance. The Hessian is p(x*)/sigma^2 (J - I). The eigenvalues of J lie in (0, 1). The largest one sets the linear rate, and iterates approach x* along its eigenvector, the principal axis of the local covariance. Off-mode Jacobians are not given.

Convergence order depends on bandwidth. It is 'nearly always linear', becomes superlinear as sigma -> 0 or sigma -> infinity, and is sublinear where modes merge. At the intermediate sigma used in practice, the rate r (distance to the mode after a step divided by before) 'can be close to 1', so convergence is slow. In image segmentation (D <= 5, N in the thousands to millions) MS typically needs I = 10 to 100 iterations per point. No rates are given for finite sigma.

Path properties of Gaussian MS on a KDE. Started far from a mode, the first steps are often large; after that they become small, consistent with linear convergence. Each iterate is a convex combination of the data, so the path stays inside their convex hull (true for any kernel with K' >= 0). Consecutive mean-shift vectors always make an angle in (-pi/2, pi/2) (cited from [29]). The mean-shift vector is proportional to grad p, but the step is not the optimal step along it.
MS basins of attraction can be curved, nonconvex and disconnected. Their boundaries can be fractal, which the paper attributes to the iterated map f rather than to the gradient-flow lines.

Convergence guarantees need nonnegative weights and kernels. In the review's words, when 'the weights or the kernels can take negative values' (elastic embedding; score-matching MS with weighted kernels) the fixed-point iteration 'need not converge'.

BMS convergence (Cheng 1995 [24]). With an infinite-support kernel such as the Gaussian, every point converges to a single point for any sigma, and the dataset diameter shrinks at least geometrically. With finite-support kernels and small sigma, several coincident clusters result. The dataset variance need not fall monotonically. Perron-Frobenius argument: P has one eigenvalue of 1 for broad kernels, and a repeated eigenvalue of 1 for non-broad kernels.

Gaussian BMS on an infinite Gaussian dataset (assumption: infinite data with a Gaussian distribution, [13]). Along each principal axis the spread evolves as s <- s/(1 + (sigma/s)^2), which converges to 0 at cubic order. Low-variance directions collapse first and the principal direction last, which produces temporarily line-shaped clusters. In Fig. 6 (cameraman, sigma = 6) this gives 7 clusters after BMS was stopped at tau = 11 by the entropy criterion; without stopping, the clusters would eventually merge into one.

Generalized BMS X <- X phi(P) on Gaussian data: each axis evolves as s <- |phi(r(s))| s. It converges iff |phi(r)| < 1 for r in (0,1) and phi(1) = 1, with order from linear to cubic and beyond. Counting both iterations and per-iteration cost, the fastest filter was the slightly over-relaxed explicit phi(P) = (1 - eta) I + eta P with eta ~ 1.25, but its runtime was 'very close' to standard BMS (eta = 1). The paper cites [15] here and gives no numbers or datasets.

Denoising (Sec. 2.6): one or two BMS iterations move noisy points toward the data manifold. Iterating longer collapses the points into clusters and destroys the manifold, so BMS must be stopped 'very early'. MBMS avoids this by removing the tangential component of each step, which preserves a spiral and ignores outliers (Fig. 3: 1,000 noisy spiral points plus 100 uniform outliers in [-30, 30]^2, same sigma for both methods).

A mode is a scale-dependent local average. As sigma -> infinity it becomes the global mean (K-modes reduces to K-means); as sigma -> 0 it becomes an individual data point (K-modes reduces to K-medoids). At intermediate sigma, modes are local averages that 'remove noise' and can be more prototypical than any single data point.

High dimensions: according to the review, KDEs 'break down'. The number of clusters jumps from one at large sigma to many 'with only a minute decrease in sigma'. On MNIST (D = 784) MS gives either one uninformative mode or many modes sitting on small groups or outliers (Fig. 7). Successful MS applications are low-dimensional (image segmentation, D <= 5). The geometry of Gaussian-mixture modes in high dimension is listed as an open problem.

Mode geometry. In 1D, the Gaussian is the only kernel that creates no new modes as sigma grows. In 2D and above, Gaussian KDEs can create modes, and an isotropic equal-sigma Gaussian mixture can have more modes than components. In the regular-simplex construction (D+1 components), D+2 modes appear in a narrow sigma window, and the lifetime of the extra barycenter mode peaks at D = 698. Modes of isotropic mixtures lie inside the convex hull of the data.

Acceleration (image segmentation only, [13],[12]). Accelerated BMS (merging collapsed clusters at each iteration, essentially no approximation error) takes about 4-5 BMS iterations at nearly any bandwidth, which is 2-4x faster than BMS and 5-60x faster than MS. Spatial-discretization MS brings the iterations per point down to nearly 1 with very small clustering error. MS-Newton hybrids run MS steps first, then switch to Newton.

Practical settings. In segmentation, reasonable bandwidths are about 1/5 of the image size. The connected-components threshold is epsilon = 0.5 pixels for MS. For BMS, epsilon = 0.01 is safe because cubic convergence makes clusters very tight.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L1: looping helps narrow Cos-Bochner more than GeGLU on recall
bearing_on_predictions.reason: The review sees per-pass gain as non-monotone in bandwidth. Convergence is superlinear as sigma -> 0 AND as sigma -> infinity, so one pass already lands near the mode and extra passes add little. Convergence is slow and linear at intermediate sigma (rate r close to 1), which is where each extra pass still makes progress. Read through MS, then, L1 holds only if Cos sigma = 4 (facts) or T = 1 (bios) falls in the intermediate regime for the actual state geometry, and nobody has measured that. My rough estimate assumes unit LN gain and random-like states, so it is only a guide: for facts (d = 128, LN norm ~11.3) the Gaussian kernel between unrelated states is about exp(-8) ~ 3e-4 at sigma = 4 and exp(-2) ~ 0.14 at sigma = 8. On that estimate sigma = 4 is near the narrow, one-step extreme, and sigma = 8 may be the regime where looping helps. The guarantees also assume normalized weights with values equal to the keys. Our Cos FFN is unnormalized: within about sigma of a key it re-writes a fixed value v_i, and farther away f is about 0. Extra passes therefore accumulate the same write rather than refining toward a state, so the MS argument for L1 does not transfer cleanly. On GeGLU the paper is silent. The small GeGLU drop (0.938/0.933/0.926) comes from one eval set of 4,096 facts, with per-run SE about 0.004, and needs seed spread before it is read as a decline.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L2: looping improves noise robustness (clean-up toward stored states) more for Cos-Bochner
bearing_on_predictions.reason: Supported in mechanism: MS/BMS is explicitly a denoiser, and one or two iterations pull noisy points toward high-density regions (Sec. 2.6). The paper also qualifies this in three ways that matter for us. (1) Clean-up goes to a MODE, not to a stored point. At intermediate or wide sigma, modes are local averages that can merge several stored facts, so a noisy state can be cleaned up to the wrong or merged state. At narrow sigma every key keeps its own attractor, but the basins are small (radius about sigma), so clean-up should work at e = 0.1 and fail at e = 0.5 unless 0.5 times |h| is still within about sigma. This predicts an interaction between noise level and bandwidth, not a uniform Cos advantage. (2) Contraction is fastest in low-variance directions and slowest along the local principal axis. In d = 128, isotropic noise is mostly off-manifold and should be removed in one pass, leaving along-manifold error. (3) In high dimension, mode structure is fragile (one mode to many modes with a tiny change of sigma). Our loop keeps the keys fixed, so it is MS rather than BMS, and BMS's collapse to a single point does not apply directly. The accuracy-under-noise measure cannot tell clean-up toward the stored state apart from drift into the right decision region.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L3: the narrow kernel has the largest per-pass Jacobian
bearing_on_predictions.reason: The answer depends on where J is evaluated. At a mode, eq. 5 gives J = Sigma(x*)/sigma^2 with eigenvalues in (0,1). J goes to 0 as sigma -> 0, but also as sigma -> infinity (J -> S/sigma^2). So the narrow kernel gives one of the two SMALLEST fixed-point Jacobians, and the largest (near 1) comes at intermediate sigma and at mode merges. At fixed points, L3 is contradicted. Off-mode, the paper gives only the fractal basin boundaries. My own derivation for the normalized Gaussian MS map gives J(x) = posterior covariance / sigma^2 at any x. Between two keys a distance Delta apart, that is about Delta^2/(4 sigma^2), which is huge for narrow sigma. So L3 can be true at boundary or pre-write states. Our probe measures J at pass INPUT states, which for K = 1 is the pre-write state, not a fixed point. For our unnormalized Cos FFN, the kernel-bump gradient scales as 1/sigma, so J_f is largest at distance about sigma from a key. At a key and far from keys, J_f is about 0, so J is about I. The task's claim that narrow bandwidth gives the smallest J at stored states holds only for a normalized MS map with values equal to the keys. For the unnormalized FFN, J at a stored key is about I (radius 1), not about 0. A median over states mixes these regimes, and two bandwidths cannot locate the non-monotone peak.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L4: looping widens Cos-Bochner T = 1's seen/held-out gap
bearing_on_predictions.reason: Weak, mechanistic support only. As sigma -> 0, each data point becomes its own mode (the K-medoids limit). At larger sigma, modes are local averages that merge nearby points and can be 'more prototypical than actual data points'. That fits the earlier finding that T = 1 stores wording and T = 2 stores wording-invariant facts. Read as MS's out-of-sample mapping (run MS on a new point and assign it to the mode it reaches), looping at narrow sigma should pull seen-template states onto their own seen-wording attractors. Held-out-template states move only if they fall inside a seen-wording basin, so the gap would widen. The paper offers no generalization evidence, and two caveats weaken the transfer. (a) In bios, every pass adds a post-norm vector of fixed RMS, so the residual iteration has no fixed point in x. Mode-seeking can only show in the direction of x. (b) Omega is trained, so T only sets the initial bandwidth, and the kernel is no longer Gaussian or stationary after training.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L5: Cos T = 2 stays wording-invariant under looping
bearing_on_predictions.reason: Consistent: wider-bandwidth modes are local averages over nearby paraphrase states, so iterating toward them should keep the representation invariant to wording. The review also implies two risks. (1) At intermediate sigma, convergence is linear with rate near 1, so K <= 4 passes may barely move the state, and L5 could hold trivially because looping does nothing. (2) In high dimension the step from many modes to few is abrupt in sigma, and iterating toward merged modes could blur distinct individuals' facts (mode merging, sublinear convergence) instead of only blurring wording. This shows up as falling held-out and seen accuracy together, not as a growing gap. BMS collapse is not expected because the keys do not move under test-time looping.

critical_gaps: This is a review: results are stated 'without proof' and come mostly from the author's own cited papers. Quantitative evidence is a handful of single illustrative examples: cameraman 50x50 with sigma = 8 (MS) and sigma = 6 (BMS), a spiral, MNIST. There are no tables, seeds, or error bars. Speed-ups (2-4x, 5-60x) are reported for image segmentation only.

Eq. 5 and the claim that eigenvalues lie in (0,1) are a linearization AT a mode, for the Gaussian kernel with one isotropic sigma. The paper says nothing quantitative about Jacobians off-mode, and off-mode is where our probe takes its pass-1 Jacobian. Strictly, Sigma(x*) is only PSD. Its rank is at most the number of points with non-negligible weight minus one, so in high dimension at narrow sigma most eigenvalues are 0 rather than in (0,1).

The convergence-order claims ('superlinear as sigma -> 0 or infinity', 'r can be close to 1' at useful sigma) are qualitative limit statements. No rate is given as a function of sigma relative to data scale, so they cannot fix where 'narrow' or 'intermediate' lies for a given dataset.
The BMS analysis with cubic convergence and s <- s/(1 + (sigma/s)^2) assumes an infinite Gaussian dataset. For finite data, the review itself notes that variance can increase at some steps.

The paper admits the high-dimensional regime is poorly understood ('KDEs break down in high dimensions'; open problem 1), and its successes are at D <= 5. Our states are d = 128 (facts) and d = 256 (bios), outside the validated regime.
The generalized-BMS finding (eta ~ 1.25 fastest) is given without numbers, datasets or a sigma range, and only for BMS, not MS.

Mapping gap 1: every guarantee needs normalized, nonnegative weights (sum_n p(n|x) = 1) and values equal to the keys, so the update is m(x) - x. The Cos-Bochner FFN computes an unnormalized sum_j k(x, x_j) v_j with learned, signed values. The review states that negative weights or kernels void convergence. An unnormalized kernel FFN cannot produce the -x term: at a stored key its Jacobian is about 0, so I + J_f is about I, and away from keys f is about 0. So 'J_f close to -I' is not what the Cos FFN does at keys.

Mapping gap 2: 'J_f close to -I' is the superlinear extreme only. Generic mode-seeking means J_f eigenvalues in (-1, 0), and at the intermediate sigma where looping would matter they are near 0 along the principal directions. Because |J - I|_2 = max(1 - lambda_i), it is about 1 for ANY high-dimensional MS (many directions with zero posterior variance). So |J - I| cannot discriminate bandwidth.

Mapping gap 3 (measurement): pre-LN or RMSNorm makes the per-pass map scale-invariant in its input. In facts, J h = h and J 1 = 1 up to LN eps; in bios, J x = x. Every measured Jacobian therefore has an eigenvalue of exactly 1, so 'spectral radius below 1' is impossible by construction. A spectral radius >= 1 cannot reject mode-seeking. Contraction can only appear in the subspace orthogonal to h (and to 1).

Mapping gap 4: in bios, Gemma's post_ffn_norm makes every pass add a vector of fixed RMS, so the looped iteration has no fixed point in x. Any decline in rel_step = |dx|/|x| can come purely from |x| growing. In facts, rel_step = |a f|/|h| shares that confound.

Mapping gap 5: the K = 1 GeGLU result (spectral radius about 3.3, rel step 1.47) is measured at the pre-write state. The review notes that MS's first steps from far away are large, and off-mode MS Jacobians can exceed 1 near basin boundaries. So these two numbers alone do not show a 'non-mode-seeking' map. The decisive quantities are the Jacobian at the end state and the size of a second pass.

Mapping gap 6: Bochner random features approximate the Gaussian kernel only up to a noise floor of about 1/sqrt(2D) per pair (D = 16,384 in facts, 4,096 in bios). At sigma = 4 or T = 1 the true kernel between unrelated states (rough estimate e^-8 to e^-16) sits below that floor. The 'narrow' RFF smoother is therefore not a narrow kernel smoother, which is exactly the regime where MS theory predicts clean one-step convergence. In facts, Adam's per-coordinate scaling also stops W_o from staying exactly in span{phi(x_j)}, so the kernel-smoother form is approximate. In bios Omega is trained, so the kernel drifts from Gaussian or stationary.

Our design confound, which the paper's framing does not fix: the facts Cos FFN (width 16,384, about 2.1M trained W_o parameters) and GeGLU (width 512, about 0.2M) differ about 10x in last-FFN capacity. A looping-gain comparison is confounded by capacity and by ceiling effects.
measures_we_lack: A tangent-space Jacobian spectrum: the spectral radius and norm of P J P, where P projects out h and the ones vector (facts LN) or x (bios RMSNorm), or else the Jacobian of the normalized map LN(h_{k+1}) wrt LN(h_k). The current spectral radius has an exact eigenvalue-1 floor from normalization (facts.py loop_probe lines 193-204; bios.py lines 686-700). Report the eigenvalue distribution (the fraction with |lambda| < 1), not only the max.

The Jacobian at the putative fixed point: at the output state h_K and after K_test = 8 passes, together with the fixed-point residual |f(LN(h_8))|/|h_8|. Today J is taken only at pass inputs, which for K = 1 is the pre-write state. Eq. 5 applies only at the fixed point.

Per-pass dynamics over K_test = 8 for every model, including K = 1-trained ones: the absolute step |dh_k|, the ratio |dh_{k+1}|/|dh_k| (MS predicts geometric decay at rate lambda_max in (0,1)), the cosine between successive steps (MS predicts positive, angle in (-pi/2, pi/2); negative means overshoot), and |h_k| itself. Relative step alone conflates a shrinking step with a growing norm, and in bios the post-norm makes |dx| constant.

The dimensionless bandwidth: the distribution of distances from each LN or RMSNorm state to its nearest stored training state, and of pairwise key distances, in units of sigma (facts) or sqrt(T sqrt(d)) (bios). For bios, also the post-training singular spectrum of the trained Omega to get the effective bandwidth. The review's predictions turn on sigma relative to data scale, and 'narrow' is currently a label, not a measurement.
An RFF-fidelity check: phi(x).phi(y) against the exact Gaussian kernel for pairs of stored states at sigma = 4/8 and T = 1/2, to see whether the narrow kernel is below the 1/sqrt(D) noise floor.

A clean-up direction measure for the noise test: after each pass, the distance from the noisy-start trajectory to the clean trajectory in LN coordinates, and the cosine between the step and (clean - noisy). Also a finer noise sweep in units of sigma, several noise draws per level (now one fixed draw), and a split into top-J-eigenvector versus remaining components (MS contracts the low-variance directions first).

An attractor census: the number of distinct end states after K_test = 8 from all eval facts, merged with an epsilon threshold as in the paper's connected-components step, and the fraction of facts whose looped endpoint lies closer to another individual's endpoint (mode merging). For bios, also the fraction of held-out-template states that end in the same person's seen-template attractor.

A test-time step-size sweep a in {0.5, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2} without retraining. An MS-like map predicts per-direction eigenvalues 1 - a(1 - lambda), with mild gains up to about a = 1.25 (generalized BMS) and divergence for a > 2/(1 - lambda_min). The current runs fix a = 1.

Normalization and bandwidth controls: a normalized kernel FFN (Nadaraya-Watson sum k v / sum k, or an explicit MS block f(x) = m(x) - x with values equal to the keys), and more than two bandwidths. The review predicts a non-monotone looping gain (small at both extremes, largest at intermediate sigma), which two bandwidths cannot resolve.

A capacity- and ceiling-matched comparison: Cos width 16,384 against GeGLU width 512 differs about 10x in last-FFN parameters. Compare looping gains at matched K = 1 accuracy and matched parameter count, and separate the test-time-K effect (K_test sweep on K = 1-trained models) from the train-time-K effect.

Seed spread and standard errors: accuracy on 4,096 eval facts has SE about 0.004 per run, so the GeGLU 0.938 -> 0.926 drop is about 3 SE on one eval set. Two seeds is thin for between-model interaction claims (L1, L2).

reads.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 3.1, Knowledge Storage and Extraction (Allen-Zhu, Li), arXiv 2309.14316v3
reads.sections_read: All of v3 from the arXiv HTML, read as plain text in full: abstract, Sec. 1-8 and Appendices A-H, including footnotes and figure captions. I also looked at the figure images that carry the numbers: Fig. 1a, 2a-c, 3, 5, 6b, 7 (= 16a), 9, 10, 12a, 12c, 16c, 17 and 18a. I did not look at these appendix panels: Fig. 2d, 11 (12 fine-tuning grids), 12b, 13, 14, 15, 16b/d, 18b and 19. Their captions say they extend figures I did read.
reads.setup:
Models: GPT2 with rotary embeddings, or a Llama-style model of the same size. 124M (12 layers, 12 heads, d 768) for bioS; 302M (12 layers, 20 heads, d 1280) for bioR; 682M (32 heads) only for one negative result. There is also GBERT, a bidirectional GPT2 trained with whole-word masked-LM. No looping or weight tying anywhere; the only thing repeated is passes over the data.

Data: N = 100k synthetic people, each with a unique 3-part name and 6 attributes drawn uniformly and independently. Birth date has 200x12x28 values; birth city 200, university 300, major 100, employer 263. Company city is fixed by the employer, and 13.7% of companies are in NY.
- bioS uses about 50 templates per attribute (46-52). The base 'single' setting gives each person one entry with a fixed sentence order and the full name only in the first sentence.
- Augmentations: multiM (M entries per person, templates resampled), permute (sentence order shuffled), fullname (pronouns replaced by the full name).
- bioR is the same people written up by Llama1-30B, with rejection sampling so all 6 attributes appear.

Training:
- Pretraining from scratch: AdamW, lr 1e-3 cosine down to 1e-4, wd 0.1, batch 96, context 512. 80k steps on bioS (about 540 passes per person), 150k steps on bioR (about 1000 passes); 200k steps for the 682M model (1350 passes).
- QA fine-tuning on half the people, test on the other half (out of distribution). LoRA on q/v (rank 2-32) plus LoRA on the embedding (rank 0-128), or full fine-tuning, 50k steps. Scoring is exact match with beam search 4.
- Mixed training: BIO plus QA for half the people from the start, QA ratio 0.8.

Probes:
- P-probe: frozen model, rank-2 LoRA on the embedding, LayerNorm and a linear head on the last layer. It reads the token just before each of the 6 attributes and predicts every attribute (6x6 tasks).
- Q-probe: input is the name alone between a start and an end token. Rank-16 LoRA on the embedding, BatchNorm and a linear head on the last-layer state at the end token.
- Probe training: AdamW, wd 0.3, 30k steps, dropout on.
- Footnote 25 implies probes are trained on N/2 people.

Every result is a single run; no seeds or error bars are reported.
key_results: Mixed training, GPT2, QA ratio 0.8, out-of-distribution QA accuracy (Fig. 1a): 86.6% on bioS single, 77.7% on bioR single. On bioS single it rises with the QA ratio: 24.5% at 0.1, 77.5% at 0.4, 87.1% at 0.6 (Fig. 10).

BIO pretraining then QA fine-tuning, bioS single, GPT2-124M, 540 passes (Fig. 2a): mean test QA is 5.7-10.5% across the whole LoRA grid. Full fine-tuning gives 7.5% test while the first-token accuracy on the fine-tuning people is 98.9%. bioR single, 302M, 1000 passes: 6.5-10.3%. bioS single, 682M, 1350 passes: 4.4-11.0%. So 'zero' in the abstract means roughly 5-11%, not 0%.

Per attribute, GPT2 bioS single after QA fine-tuning (Fig. 3): birth date 33.5%; company city 13.8% (the majority guess alone gives 13.7%); the other four 1.1-6.3% against chance of 0.3-1.0%. Birth date is the first attribute after the name in every entry.

Augmentations, GPT2 bioS, QA test mean (Fig. 3):
- single 9.7%
- single+fullname 48.9%
- single+permute1 4.4% (worse than none)
- single+permute5 70.0%
- multi2 41.1%, multi5 41.0% (no gain from 2 to 5 entries without permutation)
- multi2+permute 91.2%
- multi5+permute 96.6%
- multi5+permute+fullname 96.2%
Mixed-training counterparts: 82.5-95.7% for every row.
GPT2 bioR, QA test mean (Fig. 12a): single 10.0%, single+fullname 40.9%, multi3 88.5%, multi5 93.7%.

Llama on bioS gives much lower numbers in the middle of the range, though the paper calls the results 'similar' (Fig. 12c vs Fig. 3, Llama vs GPT2):
- single 3.5% vs 9.7%
- single+fullname 18.6% vs 48.9%
- single+permute5 41.5% vs 70.0%
- multi2+fullname 68.2% vs 84.0%
- multi5+permute 92.7% vs 96.6%

P-probe, first token, GPT2 bioS (Fig. 5):
- single: accuracy stays at baseline until the token just before the attribute, then jumps. Company name: 1.5 / 1.2 / 1.3 / 2.4% at positions 0-3 (baseline 1.5%), then 99.5% at position 4. Major: 4.7 / 4.6 / 5.4%, then 99.9%.
- multi5+permute: 99.9-100% for all six attributes from position 0 onward.
- single+permute1: rises gradually, e.g. birth month 26.1, 28.9, 32.8, 40.5, 56.8, then 100%.

Q-probe from the name alone, first token (Fig. 7):
- bioS single: birth month 63.4%, birth city 1.9% (baseline 2.5%), company name 0.2% (baseline 1.5%).
- multi5+permute: 99.8-100% on all six.
- The Q-probe tracks QA attribute by attribute. multi2: Q-probe 100 / 70.3 / 45.1 / 19.6 / 0.7 / 13.0 vs QA 100 / 71.7 / 33.1 / 26.1 / 5.2 / 14.0.
- The whole-attribute Q-probe can undershoot QA: multi5+permute university 72.6% vs 91.3%.
Dependency between attributes, bioS couple2, predicting major (Fig. 6b): about 100% once the university has appeared; 85.8-88.4% otherwise, against a base of 85.9%.

Celebrity effect, QA on the minority group (Fig. 8/17):
- bioS single+permute1: 4.4% alone, 86.8% with 100k augmented celebrities in pretraining.
- bioR single: 10.0% alone, 76.3% with celebrities, but 7.3% with WikiBook text instead.
- When the formats differ (minority uses fullname, celebrities do not), the gain is only 31.7% to 52.7%.

GBERT, masked-LM pretraining (Fig. 9): QA after fine-tuning is 3.1-39.7%, mixed training 15.7-43.6%. It works only for attributes made of independent tokens (birth date, majors that are mostly one word) and when fullname is used.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L1: looping helps narrow Cos-Bochner more than GeGLU on recall (facts task)
bearing_on_predictions.reason: The paper studies where facts are stored as the data gets more diverse. It does not study recall capacity, iterating a layer, or FFN type. Our facts task asks for attributes straight from the name, which is already the paper's 'stored on the name' regime, so the paper predicts nothing about whether looping changes recall. Fig. 2 shows only that more parameters and passes (124M to 682M, 540 to 1350 passes) do not change extraction once the storage form is set (4.4-11.0%). That is about where facts are stored, not how accurately they are recalled.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L4: looping widens Cos T = 1's seen/held-out gap (memorized wording)
bearing_on_predictions.reason: Supports the premise: the paper shows wording can be memorized almost perfectly (first-token accuracy at least 99%) while transfer stays near the floor, and links this to facts being keyed on context or template tokens instead of the name (Fig. 5 and 7). Contradicts the paper's account as an explanation of our case: our biographies already carry the paper's strongest augmentations (full name in every sentence, random sentence order, 20 training templates per person and attribute, resampled every step). Under those conditions GPT2 reaches 96.2% QA and 99.8-100% on the name-only probe (bioS multi5+permute+fullname). Cos T = 1 with AdamW memorizing (100% seen, 65% held-out) is therefore an effect of the model or optimizer, which the paper's data-only account does not cover. The paper has no evidence on whether extra iterated compute deepens template-keyed storage. Its capacity results (Fig. 2) show more capacity does not close the gap, not that it widens it.

bearing_on_predictions.prediction: L5: Cos T = 2 stays wording-invariant under looping
bearing_on_predictions.reason: Weakly consistent at K = 1: with heavily augmented data the paper finds storage on the name in both GPT2 and Llama, which matches T = 2 being wording-invariant. It says nothing about stability when a layer is iterated. Its own Llama vs GPT2 gaps of 15-30 points under the same data (e.g. single+fullname 18.6% vs 48.9%) also warn that a change of FFN or architecture can move a model between regimes, so T = 2 staying invariant under looping has to be measured, not assumed.

critical_gaps: The headline is overstated. The abstract says '0% accuracy', but Fig. 2 and 3 show 4.4-11.0% mean QA on single data. Birth date gets 33.5% because it always comes right after the name, and company city sits at the majority-guess level (13.8% vs 13.7%). The near-zero result holds for four of six attributes, not all.

Every number is a single run with no error bars. Test-set selection inflates the positive results: Appendix D reports the best test accuracy over lr/wd settings for full fine-tuning, and the best of r = 8 / r = 16 for Fig. 3 and 12. Close pairs such as multi2 41.1% vs multi5 41.0%, or multi2+fullname 84.0% vs multi5+fullname 82.4%, cannot be told apart.

'More augmentation is better' is not monotone in the paper's own data: single+permute1 (4.4%) is below single (9.7%); multi5 equals multi2 (41.0% vs 41.1%); adding fullname to multi5+permute does nothing (96.6% vs 96.2%).

The probes are only 'nearly' linear. Both add a LoRA on the embedding (rank 2 for P, rank 16 for Q) whose effect passes through the whole frozen network, so the probe can use the transformer's nonlinear computation. The Q-probe is then a constrained fine-tune on name-only input, much like the QA fine-tune it is said to explain (rank-128 embedding LoRA plus q/v LoRA). Part of the QA vs Q-probe correlation is built in. The train/test split by person is only implied (footnote 25).

The causal claim (stored on the name, therefore extractable) rests on correlation across data conditions. There is no intervention on the representation: no patching of name-token states, no ablation of attention to the template, and no auxiliary loss that forces name-keyed storage with the data held fixed.

The P-probe at the token just before an attribute is about 100% in every condition (e.g. 99.2-100% on bioS single), because it is simply the model's next-token prediction. Only earlier positions tell the cases apart, and those also see attributes already written into the same biography. 'Flawed logic' (one attribute predicting another) and 'name plus context' storage are separated only partly, by the bioS couple Venn analysis.

The effect of architecture is played down. The paper says Llama gives 'similar results', yet Llama scores 15-30 points lower than GPT2 at intermediate augmentation (Fig. 12c vs 3). The two differ in FFN (SwiGLU vs GELU MLP), normalization and more, so this sensitivity to architecture and FFN is real and never analysed. GBERT differs further still.

The optimizer (AdamW only), learning-rate schedule and training length are fixed. Training dynamics are shown only for mixed training (Fig. 1b-c), not for how storage location forms during BIO pretraining. The paper cannot tell data effects apart from optimization effects. Our Muon vs AdamW result suggests the optimizer matters.

The extraction test needs a new QA format to be learned by fine-tuning, so the failure mixes 'where the fact is stored' with 'whether the new format can be bound to it'. The celebrity format-mismatch result (52.7% vs 86.8%) shows that extraction depends on the format, not only on storage on the name.

The data have a built-in confound: company city is a deterministic function of company, which the paper acknowledges. Attributes are uniform and independent, and the name-length tokenization is uncontrolled. The setting is a 124-682M model with N = 100k people and at most 5 entries per person; the far more varied setting of our biographies is never tested.
measures_we_lack: Probes on the name tokens placed where looping can matter. The loop is in the last layer's FFN, so its output at name positions is read only by the unembedding; no later attention can carry it to the value position. Looping therefore cannot 'move facts onto the name' in a form the value prediction can use. Probe the name's last token at the output of every layer below the looped FFN, including the input to the loop, for models trained at K = 1, 2, 4. Train the probe on half the people and test on the other half. Use only the first sentence of each biography (or a name-only input) so attributes copied from earlier sentences cannot leak in. Changing K at test time cannot change these lower-layer states, so the comparison has to be between training K values.

A cross-template P-probe at the position that predicts the value, read at the input to the looped FFN. Train on seen-template positions and test on held-out-frame positions of the same people. The plain 'token just before the value' probe is about 100% even for memorized data (paper Fig. 5), so only the transfer version tells the arms apart.

A test of what the narrow kernel sees. At the Cos layer input, per pass k: the kernel similarity exp(-||x_held - x_seen||^2 / (2 T sqrt d)) between a held-out-frame query and the nearest seen-frame query for the same person and attribute. Also the similarity for same person / different frame vs same frame / different person. This tests directly whether T = 1 treats a new wording as a new point, and whether looping pushes the two apart.

Held-out accuracy by sentence position within the biography (first sentence vs later ones), the paper's 'flawed logic' check. If later sentences score much higher, the model keys facts on attributes it has already seen instead of the name.

A per-attribute breakdown with chance baselines, and first-token vs whole-value accuracy. The paper's attributes range from 33.5% to 1.1% inside one model, and our birth date is three independent tokens, which the paper finds behave differently (GBERT).

Seen and held-out accuracy over training for each K, not only at the end. The paper's Fig. 1b-c shows in-distribution accuracy rises well before transfer does, so a gap at a single checkpoint can be a timing artifact.

At least 2-3 seeds per arm, and no test-set best-of selection. The paper is single-run, and our GeGLU differences (0.938 / 0.933 / 0.926 for K = 1 / 2 / 4) are 0.005-0.012 apart, which cannot be read without seed variance.

A capacity- and compute-matched control without tied weights: an untied stack of K FFNs, or a wider FFN, in the last block. The paper finds more capacity does not move storage (Fig. 2), so any looping effect needs to be shown to come from tying and iteration, not from extra compute.

A data-diversity axis. Run GeGLU and Cos T = 1 / T = 2 with 1 or 5 training templates per person and attribute, a fixed sentence order, and the name only in the first sentence. That places our arms on the paper's curve and tests whether Cos T = 1's memorization works like the paper's data-poor failure, and whether looping's effect depends on data diversity.

Causal interventions instead of probe correlation alone: patch name-token states between people, or ablate attention from the value position to the frame tokens, and measure the effect on seen and held-out accuracy at each K.

The optimizer as a crossed factor under looping (AdamW vs Muon, for Cos T = 1 and T = 2). The paper fixes AdamW, while our earlier result shows the optimizer decides between memorized wording and invariant facts.

synthesis:
Source status. All eight notes have read_end_to_end true, so no note needs a flag. Values marked "derived" were calculated by the note authors with LayerNorm gain 1.

1. Predictions

L1. The evidence is weak and runs from neutral to negative. Saunshi et al. (2502.17416) find that looping raises closed-book recall only as much as it lowers perplexity. Closed-book %Gap is 37-58 and perplexity %Gap is 34-48, and alpha_loop/alpha_base is 0.5 for both. All their runs are single seed. Ouro (2510.25741) reports no capacity gain from looping: loop 1 and loop 4 both store about 2 bits/param. That result comes from one scatter plot at saturation. We store 0.27 (GeGLU) and 0.037 (Cos) bits per trainable parameter, so it does not apply to us. Hopfield (2008.02217) and Kernel Memory Networks (2208.09416) predict that sharp kernels retrieve in one update. Mean-shift (1503.00687) puts the largest gain per pass at intermediate bandwidth. The notes disagree on sigma = 4. The Hopfield note puts it in the transition band (derived). The mean-shift note puts it at the narrow extreme (derived).

L2. The evidence is mixed and comes from theory only. Hopfield proves contraction only within radius 1/(beta N M), which is negligible at N = 32,768. Kernel Memory Networks gives one-step recovery within radius r and no gain from later passes. The derived radii are e = 0.55 (sigma = 4) and 1.73 (sigma = 8), so our noise grid 0.1/0.25/0.5 is inside both. DrDAM (2410.24153) shows clean-up only for near queries. Every one of these results needs an auto-associative map. Our FFN is hetero-associative and has no -h term.

L3. The literature contradicts L3 at stored states and supports it at basin boundaries. Hopfield gives J = beta Var_p[x]. J is near zero at a stored pattern and equals beta Delta/2 at a boundary between two patterns (derived: 2.4-4 for sigma = 4, 0.6-1 for sigma = 8). Mean-shift eq. 5 gives eigenvalues in (0, 1) at a mode. Four notes derive a flaw in our probe. Pre-LN gives J h = h, so our spectral radius is at least 1 by construction.

L4. The support is weak and only mechanistic. Narrow kernels make small basins, so held-out states outside them get no pull (Kernel Memory Networks, mean-shift). Allen-Zhu and Li (2309.14316) link memorized wording to poor data. Transfer is 9.7% on bioS single and 96.2% with full names, sentence permutation and five entries per person. Our bios task already has these augmentations, so the T = 1 effect comes from the model or the optimizer. In Ouro, looping closes generalization gaps on 3-hop QA (62/33/14% for loop 4/2/1). Saunshi points the same way.

L5. The support is conditional. Hopfield Lemma A12 makes cluster averages stable when beta m_max^2 <= 1. A derived DrDAM simulation shows the risk: at beta <= 30 and K = 500, every query collapses to one centroid. Mean-shift predicts slow convergence at intermediate bandwidth, so L5 can hold only because looping does nothing. Ouro loses accuracy past the trained depth: 1.4B MMLU is 67.45 at T = 4 and 64.49 at T = 8. Score K_test = K_train and K_test > K_train separately.

2. Mechanisms

For a larger kernel gain: iteration helps in a transition band where the fixed point is correct and contracts slowly (Hopfield, mean-shift). Far from stored keys, the unnormalized kernel output goes to zero, so extra passes do not drift. GeGLU expands (radius 3.3). Sigma = 4 stores 32,768 facts on 16,384 features, which is at the zero-margin load limit (Kernel Memory Networks, derived). Extra passes add effective features.

Against a larger kernel gain: narrow kernels finish in one step. A hetero-associative map has no stored fixed points, so the writes add up across passes. Wide kernels merge modes (DrDAM, mean-shift). The random-feature noise floor is about 1/sqrt(2D) and is larger than the narrow kernel's values between different states. So "narrow" Cos does not act as a narrow smoother (DrDAM, mean-shift). In bios, post_ffn_norm adds a write of fixed RMS on each pass, so no fixed point exists (Labovich, 2604.15259). Untied depth beats tied depth (Ouro Table 18, gaps 0.017-0.039).

3. Missing measures, ranked by value per GPU-minute

Evaluation only, on existing checkpoints:
1. Tangent-space Jacobian with h and the ones vector projected out. Add the share of branch eigenvalues with |1 + lambda| < 1.
2. Run loop_probe in /home/user/rcdltesting/rcdl/facts.py over every pass up to K_test = 8 or 16. Log |h_k|, step size, step cosine, accuracy per pass and prediction flips.
3. Dilution control: head(ln_f(h0 + n + sum_k f_k(clean))). Use several noise draws, e up to 2, and noise at K_test != K_train.
4. Geometry in kernel units: effective beta with the learned LN gain, distances to the nearest stored state in sigma units, and how well the random features match the kernel.
5. Test-time step size a in {0.5, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2}.

New runs, 2-15 minutes each:
6. Three or more seeds per cell. Log training loss at each eval step for Saunshi isoplots. The GeGLU drop is 1.2 points, about 3 binomial SE on 4,096 facts. Bios Cos seeds differ by 9 points.
7. An untied iso-FLOP arm (K separate FFNs) to get %Gap per FFN type.
8. A lower LR and gradient clipping at K = 4 (Ouro).
9. A sigma sweep {2, 3, 4, 6, 8} to find a gain that peaks at one bandwidth.

4. What no paper tests

No paper loops a single tied FFN; Ouro and Saunshi loop whole blocks. No paper compares FFN types under looping. The four kernel papers iterate an auto-associative update that replaces the state. None iterates a residual hetero-associative update behind LayerNorm. None trains a readout on random features: DrDAM sums the features, and the SDM readout in Kernel Memory Networks is one-shot. None adds noise to the state or measures per-pass Jacobians in a trained transformer. None tests K_test above a K_train that has loss only on the final pass: Saunshi evaluates at the trained depth, Ouro supervises every step, and Labovich trains on random depths. None tests invariance to wording under looping, or how the optimizer interacts with it (Allen-Zhu uses only AdamW). Ouro measures capacity at 1000 exposures. We test 39 exposures (facts) and 236 (bios).
